items.q: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman on denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 3 years abruptly discontinues the injections. Eight months after her last dose, she presents with severe back pain due to multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures. To avoid this known rebound effect, which protocol should be instituted upon stopping denosumab?
o: Transition to an antiresorptive agent such as zoledronate approximately 6 months after the last dose
Institute an obligatory 2- to 3-year drug holiday
Re-evaluate DXA at 1 year and start raloxifene only if T-score falls
items.e: Discontinuing denosumab causes a rebound surge in bone turnover, rapid bone mineral density loss, and an increased risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures within months. Denosumab should never be stopped without follow-on antiresorptive therapy, typically an infusion of zoledronate given about 6 months after the last denosumab injection.
items.note: Accurate, clinically critical concept supported directly by trial data and clinical guidelines.

items.q: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates such as alendronate and zoledronate reduce bone resorption predominantly by inhibiting which of the following biochemical targets?
o: Farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway
Carbonic anhydrase type II in the osteoclast ruffled border
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases essential for osteoclast ruffled border maintenance and survival, leading to osteoclast apoptosis.
items.note: Classic high-yield pharmacology question with clear, unambiguous biochemical mechanism.

items.q: A 65-year-old woman with severe postmenopausal osteoporosis (lumbar spine T-score -3.4) and a recent vertebral fragility fracture is evaluated for osteoanabolic treatment. Which of the following findings is an absolute contraindication to initiating teriparatide?
o: Prior external beam skeletal radiation therapy
items.e: Teriparatide is contraindicated in patients with prior skeletal radiation, Paget disease, unexplained elevated alkaline phosphatase, open epiphyses, bone metastases, or pre-existing hypercalcaemia due to increased baseline risk of osteosarcoma or hypercalcaemic crises.
items.note: Factually sound, differentiating key contraindications of teriparatide from other osteoporosis drugs.

items.q: According to the revised ASBMR Task Force case definition for atypical femoral fractures (AFF), which of the following is classified as a MINOR feature rather than a major feature?
o: Origin at the lateral cortex with substantially transverse orientation
Localised periosteal or endosteal thickening ('beaking') at the fracture site
Non-comminuted or minimally comminuted fracture line
items.e: The 5 major features of atypical femoral fractures include minimal trauma, lateral cortical origin with transverse orientation, complete/incomplete extension without comminution, and localised cortical beaking/thickening. Minor features include prodromal thigh or groin pain, diaphyseal cortical thickening, and bilaterality.
items.note: Directly tests the ASBMR case definition criteria, a frequent point of assessment in superspeciality exams.

items.q: Romosozumab is a dual-action monoclonal antibody targeting sclerostin that promotes bone formation while decreasing bone resorption. Based on clinical trials, it is contraindicated in patients with:
o: Estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min
Myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months
Pre-existing osteopenia with prior deep venous thrombosis
Unexplained elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase
items.e: In the ARCH trial, romosozumab significantly reduced fracture risk but demonstrated an imbalance in serious cardiovascular adverse events (myocardial infarction and stroke). Consequently, it is contraindicated in patients who have had a myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding 12 months.
items.note: Well-tested guideline contraindication from landmark trial results (ARCH).

items.q: In which landmark clinical trial did an annual infusion of zoledronic acid (5 mg IV) administered after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture demonstrate a significant reduction in all-cause mortality as well as new clinical fractures?
items.e: The HORIZON-RFT (Recurrent Fracture Trial) evaluated annual 5 mg zoledronic acid infusions initiated within 90 days of surgical fixation of a low-trauma hip fracture. It demonstrated a 35% reduction in new clinical fractures and a 28% reduction in all-cause mortality.
items.note: Landmark trial identifying unique mortality reduction benefit of zoledronate in orthopaedic fracture care.

items.q: Regarding sequential osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, which of the following drug transitions causes a progressive or transient loss of bone mineral density, particularly at the hip, as demonstrated in the DATA-Switch trial?
o: Switching from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy
items.e: The DATA-Switch study showed that transitioning patients from denosumab to teriparatide monotherapy leads to a transient or progressive decline in BMD, especially at cortical-rich sites like the hip. Conversely, anabolic therapy followed by an antiresorptive agent (teriparatide followed by denosumab) preserves and further increases BMD.
items.note: High-yield sequencing question supported directly by the DATA-Switch trial.

items.q: According to the ASBMR guidelines on osteoporosis management, at what treatment duration should low-to-moderate risk patients routinely be reassessed for a bisphosphonate 'drug holiday'?
o: After 5 years of oral or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 3 years of oral or 5 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 2 years of oral or 1 year of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
After 10 years of oral or 6 years of intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
items.e: The ASBMR Task Force recommends reassessing fracture risk after 5 years of oral bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronate). If the patient is not at high risk (femoral neck T-score > -2.5 and no incident fractures), a drug holiday of 2 to 3 years can be considered.
items.note: Standard guideline timeline tested regularly across metabolic bone disease exams.

items.q: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute severe neck pain, rigid cervical stiffness, and a low-grade fever mimicking meningitis. Cervical CT reveals curvilinear calcification around the odontoid process involving the transverse atlantal ligament (crowned dens syndrome). Analysis of synovial fluid from a concomitant acute arthritis of her knee is most likely to demonstrate which type of crystal?
o: Needle-shaped crystals with strongly negative birefringence
Rhomboid-shaped crystals with weakly positive birefringence
Non-birefringent crystal aggregates staining positive with alizarin red S
Bipyramidal envelope-shaped crystals with positive birefringence
items.e: Crowned dens syndrome is an axial manifestation of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) caused by CPP crystal deposition around the odontoid process. CPPD crystals are characteristically rhomboid- or rod-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised light microscopy.
items.note: Accurate, high-yield clinical vignette directly covered in standard orthopaedic references and notes.

items.q: Which of the following radiographic abnormalities is characteristic of chronic tophaceous gout and helps distinguish it from rheumatoid arthritis?
o: Punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges
Marginal erosions localized strictly to synovial bare areas
items.e: Chronic gout classically produces punched-out juxta-articular erosions with sclerotic borders and overhanging margins (Martel sign or 'rat-bite' erosions). In contrast to rheumatoid arthritis, gout characteristically preserves the joint space until late stages and lacks periarticular osteopenia.
items.note: Classic radiological differentiator between gout and rheumatoid arthritis, perfectly aligned with syllabus.

items.q: A 48-year-old man presents with acute pseudogout of the right knee. Because he is younger than 60 years, he is screened for metabolic predispositions. Which of the following conditions represents one of the classic '4 H's' associated with calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease?
items.e: The classic metabolic associations ('4 H's') that predispose to CPPD disease are Haemochromatosis, Hyperparathyroidism, Hypomagnesaemia, and Hypophosphatasia (characterised by low alkaline phosphatase). Patients under 60 years presenting with CPPD should be screened for these secondary causes.
items.note: Standard high-yield exam mnemonic and clinical screening guideline.

items.q: A 55-year-old man with severe, refractory chronic tophaceous gout is being evaluated for therapy with pegloticase. Which of the following baseline laboratory tests is mandatory before starting pegloticase to prevent life-threatening haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia?
items.e: Pegloticase is a recombinant uricase that oxidises uric acid to allantoin and produces hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct. Patients with G6PD deficiency are at high risk of severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, making baseline G6PD screening essential before therapy.
items.note: Crucial pharmacogenomic safety step tested frequently in superspeciality exams.

items.q: In the staging of calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff described by Uhthoff, during which stage does the patient typically experience the most severe, excruciating pain?
items.e: The resorptive phase of the calcific stage is characterised by vascular and macrophage invasion with a toothpaste-like deposit under high pressure. This marked inflammatory reaction makes the resorptive phase the most painful clinical stage, often leading to spontaneous bursal rupture.
items.note: Standard Campbell-referenced Uhthoff staging question.

items.q: A 52-year-old man presents with an acute gout flare of the first metatarsophalangeal joint within the past 12 hours. Based on the AGREE trial protocol and standard guidelines, which low-dose oral colchicine regimen is recommended for acute flare management?
o: 0.5 mg every 2 hours until diarrhoea or pain relief occurs
1.2 mg stat, followed by 0.6 mg one hour later
1.0 mg twice daily for 5 consecutive days
0.6 mg every 4 hours up to a maximum of 6 mg on day 1
items.e: The AGREE trial established that low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg immediately, followed by 0.6 mg one hour later, then maintenance dosing) provides equivalent anti-inflammatory efficacy to high-dose regimens with significantly fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects.
items.note: Accurate guideline-based pharmacotherapy question directly supported by notes.

items.q: Under compensated polarised light microscopy, which optical characteristic correctly identifies monosodium urate (MSU) crystals?
o: Blue coloration when aligned parallel to the compensator axis (positive birefringence)
Yellow coloration when aligned perpendicular to the compensator axis (negative birefringence)
Blue coloration when aligned perpendicular to the compensator axis (positive birefringence)
Yellow coloration when aligned parallel to the compensator axis (negative birefringence)
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and show strong negative birefringence; they appear yellow when aligned parallel to the slow axis of the compensator and turn blue when perpendicular. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate crystals are weakly positively birefringent and turn blue when parallel.
items.note: Foundational diagnostic question in crystal arthropathy with unequivocal optical physics facts.

items.q: On musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of an inflamed joint, the 'double contour sign' is characteristic of which underlying pathology?
o: Monosodium urate crystals coating the outer surface of hyaline cartilage
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals embedded within the mid-substance of hyaline cartilage
Basic calcium phosphate deposition within the deep substance of the rotator cuff tendon
Linear calcification along the triangular fibrocartilage complex of the wrist
items.e: The 'double contour sign' on ultrasound is produced by a hyperechoic band of monosodium urate crystals coating the superficial surface of articular hyaline cartilage, overlying the deeper hyperechoic subchondral bone. In CPPD, crystal deposition occurs within the cartilage layer rather than on its surface.
items.note: Standard ultrasound sign in rheumatology and orthopaedics, unambiguous and directly referenced.

items.q: A 62-year-old man presents with deep, aching pelvic pain that is worse at night. Radiographs reveal coarse trabecular thickening and an enlarged iliopectineal line ("brim sign"). Genetic analysis identifies a mutation in the SQSTM1 gene encoding p62. This protein plays a critical regulatory role in which of the following osteoclastic signalling pathways?
items.e: SQSTM1 encodes sequestosome-1 (p62), an important scaffold protein in the RANK/NF-kappa-B pathway of osteoclasts. Mutations in SQSTM1 are found in approximately 40% of familial and 5-10% of sporadic cases of Paget disease.
items.note: Accurate, textbook-standard molecular genetics question for Paget disease.

items.q: A 74-year-old woman with active polyostotic Paget disease sustains an acute, displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture following a minor fall. What is the recommended definitive management for this specific injury in pagetic bone?
o: Dynamic hip screw with a derotation screw
items.e: Femoral neck fractures in pagetic bone carry an exceptionally high rate of non-union and delayed union with internal fixation. Therefore, arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty) is the preferred management rather than osteosynthesis.
items.note: Accurate and directly supported by Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics and notes.

items.q: The landmark PRISM trial (Langston et al., 2010) evaluated intensive bisphosphonate therapy aimed at normalising serum alkaline phosphatase versus symptom-directed therapy in Paget disease. What did this trial establish?
o: Intensive therapy significantly reduced fracture risk and the need for orthopaedic surgery
Intensive therapy arrested the progression of sensorineural deafness
Intensive therapy significantly improved clinical quality of life and pain scores
There was no clinical benefit in treating asymptomatic patients simply to normalise alkaline phosphatase
items.e: The PRISM trial demonstrated that intensive bisphosphonate treatment aiming to normalise ALP did not reduce fractures, orthopaedic surgery, hearing loss, or improve quality of life compared with symptomatic treatment. Consequently, international guidelines do not recommend treating asymptomatic Paget disease purely to normalise biochemical markers.
items.note: Crucial landmark trial well known in superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 54-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on maintenance haemodialysis sustains a low-energy metatarsal fracture. Transiliac bone biopsy demonstrates low bone turnover, diminished cellular activity, and reduced osteoid volume without aluminium accumulation. Which histological subtype is currently the commonest form of renal osteodystrophy in this setting?
items.e: Adynamic bone disease has become the commonest histological subtype of renal osteodystrophy in dialysis patients. It is characterised by low bone turnover and suppressed parathyroid hormone levels, often exacerbated by dialysis, diabetes, and over-suppression from calcium and active vitamin D therapy.
items.note: Factually robust and matches modern nephrology and metabolic orthopaedic teaching.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with persistent thigh pain and is diagnosed with an incomplete lateral subtrochanteric pseudofracture. Laboratory evaluation shows an abnormally low total serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) along with elevated urinary phosphoethanolamine. Which of the following treatments is strictly CONTRAINDICATED in this condition?
items.e: The patient has adult hypophosphatasia (mutation in ALPL). Bisphosphonates are pyrophosphate analogues that further inhibit bone mineralisation, worsening the mineralisation defect and predisposing to atypical or complete fractures; they are strictly contraindicated.
items.note: Standard contraindication pearl in metabolic bone disease.

items.q: A 4-year-old child with autism and a highly restricted diet presents with limb pain, irritability, and painful subperiosteal swelling. Radiographs reveal a dense zone of provisional calcification (white line of Frankel) and an underlying radiolucent Trummerfeld zone. What is the fundamental cellular mechanism underlying this bone disorder?
o: Defective osteoid production due to impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine
Impaired mineralisation of newly formed osteoid caused by calcium-phosphate deficiency
Hyperactive osteoclastic bone resorption driven by circulating PTHrP
Inhibition of hydroxyapatite crystal formation by accumulated inorganic pyrophosphate
items.e: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes defective hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis, leading to osteoblast dysfunction and failure of osteoid production. It is a defect in osteoid formation, not a mineralisation defect.
items.note: Classic distinction between scurvy (osteoid production failure) and rickets (mineralisation failure).

items.q: A 52-year-old man from an endemic region presents with axial stiffness, reduced chest expansion, and progressive compressive myelopathy. Radiographs reveal diffuse osteosclerosis of the spine and pelvis. Which of the following imaging features is characteristic of skeletal fluorosis and helps distinguish it from other osteosclerotic entities?
o: Subperiosteal resorption on the radial aspect of the middle phalanges
Expansion of the vertebral body with thick peripheral cortices ("picture frame" vertebra)
Calcification and ossification of the interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg
Sclerotic endplate bands with a radiolucent central vertebral body ("rugger-jersey" spine)
items.e: Skeletal fluorosis typically manifests with diffuse osteosclerosis along with prominent calcification and ossification of ligaments and interosseous membranes of the forearm and leg. Subperiosteal resorption indicates hyperparathyroidism, picture-frame vertebrae indicate Paget disease, and rugger-jersey spine indicates renal osteodystrophy.
items.note: Accurate diagnostic discriminator high-yield for Indian superspeciality exams.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman is found to have asymptomatic hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, and an elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) level consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is planned. Which anatomical site demonstrates the greatest preferential loss of bone mineral density in this condition?
items.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism preferentially causes cortical bone catabolism over trabecular bone loss. Consequently, bone mineral density drops most dramatically at cortical-predominant sites such as the distal radius (forearm), while trabecular sites like the lumbar spine are relatively preserved.
items.note: Standard endocrinology/orthopaedic guideline fact for DXA scanning in primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: During surgical dislocation of the hip via the Ganz approach, safe preservation of the deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) relies on its consistent anatomical path. What is the relationship of this vessel to the surrounding musculature?
o: It runs anterior to the obturator externus and posterior to the short external rotators
It passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators
It passes superior to the piriformis and anterior to the gluteus minimus
It courses inferior to the quadratus femoris and superficial to the obturator internus
items.e: The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) passes posterior to the obturator externus and anterior to the short external rotators (gemelli and obturator internus). This precise relationship forms the anatomical basis of the Ganz surgical dislocation approach, preserving femoral head perfusion.
items.note: Anatomically precise, fully supported by Campbell's and the reference text.

items.q: Under the ARCO 2019 classification system, which criteria must be met to define glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH)?
o: Cumulative dose over 500 mg prednisolone equivalent in 1 month; diagnosed within 6 months
Cumulative dose over 1 g prednisolone equivalent in 6 months; diagnosed within 1 year
Cumulative dose over 2 g prednisolone (or equivalent) within a 3-month period; diagnosed within 2 years
Cumulative dose over 5 g prednisolone equivalent within 1 year; diagnosed within 3 years
items.e: The ARCO 2019 criteria define glucocorticoid-associated ONFH as a history of over 2 g of prednisolone (or equivalent) administered within a 3-month timeframe, with osteonecrosis diagnosed within 2 years of exposure in the absence of other risk factors.
items.note: Accurate criteria testing an important current guideline fact.

items.q: A 36-year-old male with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with deep groin pain after high-dose corticosteroid therapy. Plain radiographs of the pelvis are unremarkable. Which MRI feature, if present, is pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: A T2 double-line sign consisting of an inner high-signal band and an outer low-signal band
Diffuse marrow oedema extending from the femoral head down into the intertrochanteric line
A subchondral low-signal fracture line that is convex toward the articular surface
Homogeneous high T1 signal intensity throughout the entire femoral epiphysis
items.e: On T2-weighted MRI, the 'double-line sign' is pathognomonic for osteonecrosis of the femoral head. It consists of an inner high-signal line of hyperaemic granulation tissue adjacent to an outer low-signal line of sclerotic bone.
items.note: High-yield, pathognomonic diagnostic sign tested cleanly.

items.q: A 32-year-old man has pre-collapse osteonecrosis of the femoral head. To assess the risk of subchondral collapse, the modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle is measured on MRI. Which necrotic angle threshold designates a 'high risk' of collapse?
items.e: The modified Kerboul combined necrotic angle sums the necrotic arcs on mid-coronal and mid-sagittal MRI. An angle under 190 degrees represents low risk, 190–239 degrees indicates intermediate risk, and 240 degrees or greater designates a high risk of collapse.
items.note: Standard prognostic classification threshold in hip preservation surgery.

items.q: During core decompression of the femoral head for pre-collapse osteonecrosis, which technical error is most directly responsible for creating a stress riser that predisposes to an iatrogenic subtrochanteric fracture?
o: Starting the lateral cortical entry hole below the level of the lesser trochanter
Advancing the drill bit to within 3 to 5 mm of the subchondral bone plate
Employing multiple small-diameter (3 mm) drillings instead of a single 8–10 mm trephine
Failing to penetrate the subchondral articular cartilage during drilling
items.e: The entry point on the lateral femoral cortex for core decompression must be at or above the level of the lesser trochanter. An entry placed below the lesser trochanter creates a major stress riser in the subtrochanteric region, leading to post-operative subtrochanteric fracture.
items.note: Critical technical pearl frequently emphasized in surgical operative texts.

items.q: A 29-year-old woman in her 34th week of pregnancy presents with acute left hip pain. Radiographs demonstrate subtle regional osteopenia. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema throughout the femoral head and neck extending into the intertrochanteric region, with no focal subchondral band or double-line sign. What is the management of choice?
o: Urgent core decompression combined with autologous bone marrow aspirate concentrate
Protected weight bearing and analgesia with observation
items.e: The presentation and imaging are classic for transient osteoporosis of the hip, which typically occurs in the third trimester of pregnancy and shows diffuse marrow oedema without a focal subchondral band or double line. It is self-limiting over 6–12 months, and management is conservative with protected weight bearing to prevent femoral neck fracture.
items.note: Important clinical scenario distinguishing transient osteoporosis from true osteonecrosis.

items.q: A 64-year-old woman presents with sudden, severe medial knee pain and night pain. Weight-bearing radiographs show subtle focal flattening of the medial femoral condyle. What is a well-established clinicopathological feature of spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK / SIFK)?
o: It is characterised by multiple bilateral lesions extending into the metaphysis and diaphysis
It is a true primary ischaemic necrosis that most commonly affects patients under 45 years of age
Lesions involving under 40% of condylar width invariably collapse and require total knee arthroplasty
It represents a subchondral insufficiency fracture and is frequently associated with a medial meniscus posterior root tear
items.e: Spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee (SONK) is pathologically a subchondral insufficiency fracture of the knee (SIFK) rather than primary ischaemic necrosis. It classically affects women over 55–60 years and is frequently associated with posterior root tears of the medial meniscus.
items.note: Crucial modern orthopaedic concept distinguishing SONK from secondary AVN.

items.q: Six weeks following internal fixation of a Hawkins type II talar neck fracture, an AP ankle radiograph shows a band of subchondral radiolucency beneath the articular surface of the talar dome (Hawkins sign). What does this finding indicate?
o: Imminent mechanical collapse of the talar dome
Complete resorption of the subchondral bone secondary to deep joint infection
Preserved vascularity to the talar dome resulting in disuse osteopenia
Late failure of fracture union requiring revision arthrodesis
items.e: Hawkins sign is a subchondral radiolucent band beneath the talar dome visible on AP radiographs 6–8 weeks post-injury. It confirms preserved talar blood supply, as subchondral disuse bone resorption requires active local vascularity.
items.note: Classic and definitive examination concept in foot and ankle trauma.

items.q: A 12-year-old child presents with limping and hip pain, diagnosed with Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE). Disruption of the physis in this condition typically occurs primarily through which zone?
items.e: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), Rickets, and standard Salter-Harris fractures predominantly occur through the hypertrophic zone (specifically the zone of provisional calcification), which is the mechanically weakest region of the growth plate.
items.note: Accurate, clean single-best-answer question supported directly by reference notes and standard orthopaedic literature.

items.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe juvenile osteoporosis and visual impairment due to ocular vascular developmental defects. Genetic analysis reveals a loss-of-function mutation in the low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) gene. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
items.e: Loss-of-function mutations in LRP5 impair Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome. In contrast, gain-of-function LRP5 mutations lead to high bone mass, loss of sclerostin (SOST) causes sclerosteosis/Van Buchem disease, and RUNX2 mutations cause cleidocranial dysplasia.
items.note: Factually accurate, unambiguous, high-yield bone biology question with perfect distractor set.

items.q: A 30-year-old male sustains a displaced midshaft femoral fracture and undergoes reamed intramedullary nailing. How does cortical bone blood flow change immediately following reaming of the medullary canal?
o: Flow reverses from centrifugal to centripetal, relying on periosteal supply
Flow reverses from centripetal to centrifugal, relying on endosteal supply
Endosteal flow increases fourfold with complete cessation of periosteal flow
Both endosteal and periosteal blood flow cease completely
items.e: Normal cortical bone blood flow is centrifugal (inside-to-outside), supplied primarily by the high-pressure endosteal nutrient system (inner two-thirds). Displaced fractures or reaming disrupt the endosteal supply, reversing blood flow to centripetal (outside-to-inside) as the periosteal supply (outer one-third) takes over.
items.note: Core applied basic science concept with exact answer supported by notes and orthopaedic standard texts.

items.q: A 6-month-old infant with osteopetrosis is found to have a homozygous mutation in the TCIRG1 gene encoding the a3 subunit of the vacuolar H+ ATPase proton pump. This specific defect directly impairs bone resorption by disrupting the function of which osteoclast structure?
items.e: The vacuolar H+ ATPase proton pump is localized to the ruffled border of osteoclasts to acidify the resorption compartment. Mutations in TCIRG1 or CLCN7 disrupt proton pump and chloride channel function at the ruffled border, preventing mineral dissolution and causing osteopetrosis.
items.note: High-yield subspeciality question on osteoclast biology with exact structure-function coupling.

items.q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman with osteoporosis starts antiresorptive therapy. To monitor treatment adherence and early biological response, which pair of turnover markers is recommended by the IOF and IFCC as standard reference markers?
o: Serum bone-specific ALP and urinary hydroxyproline
items.e: The International Osteoporosis Foundation (IOF) and International Federation of Clinical Chemistry (IFCC) recommend serum procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (P1NP) as the standard formation marker and serum C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX) as the standard resorption marker.
items.note: Standard guideline consensus question testing reference markers in bone metabolism.

items.q: A 35-year-old male undergoes the first-stage procedure of the Masquelet induced-membrane technique for a 7 cm segmental tibial defect using a PMMA spacer. At what timeframe does the bioactivity and growth factor release of the induced membrane peak for placing the secondary bone graft?
items.e: In the Masquelet induced-membrane technique, the foreign body membrane formed around the PMMA spacer reaches peak vascularity and bioactivity (releasing VEGF, TGF-beta, and BMP-2) between 4 and 8 weeks, which is the optimal window for secondary cancellous autografting.
items.note: Important clinical technique question with precise, universally accepted surgical timeframe.

items.q: Bone exhibits piezoelectric properties in response to mechanical strain. Which of the following correctly describes the electrical polarity created during bending load and its corresponding cellular effect?
o: Tension side is electropositive, stimulating bone formation
Compression side is electropositive, stimulating bone resorption
Tension side is electronegative, stimulating bone formation
Compression side is electronegative, stimulating bone formation
items.e: Under mechanical bending strain, the compression side of bone becomes electronegative, which stimulates osteoblastic bone formation. The tension side becomes electropositive, promoting osteoclastic bone resorption (providing the basis for cathode-based electrical bone stimulation).
items.note: Classic bone mechanics concept testing exact polarity-cell response coupling.

items.q: A spine surgeon evaluates recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) for off-label use in anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). Which severe complication led to a specific FDA warning against using rhBMP-2 in this region?
items.e: rhBMP-2 can induce marked local inflammatory soft-tissue swelling and seroma formation. In anterior cervical spine surgery, this swelling can cause life-threatening airway compromise and severe dysphagia, prompting an FDA safety warning.
items.note: High-yield pharmacology/biology safety question based on explicit regulatory warnings.

items.q: Which parameter increases in articular cartilage during normal physiological ageing, in contrast to early osteoarthritis?
items.e: Keratan sulfate content increases with normal physiological ageing, which decreases the chondroitin to keratan sulfate ratio. In contrast, early osteoarthritis shows decreased keratan sulfate, increased chondroitin-4 sulfate, increased water content, and increased matrix permeability.
items.note: Accurate, highly tested exam distinction between physiological cartilage ageing and early osteoarthritis.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete undergoes microfracture for a full-thickness chondral defect on the medial femoral condyle. Which predominant tissue type forms to repair the defect following marrow stimulation?
o: Fibrocartilage composed primarily of Type I collagen
Hyaline cartilage composed primarily of Type II collagen
Elastic cartilage composed of Type II collagen and elastin
Calcified cartilage rich in Type X collagen
items.e: Marrow stimulation procedures breach the subchondral bone plate, releasing bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells that form a clot maturing into fibrocartilage (composed mostly of type I collagen). Fibrocartilage is mechanically inferior to hyaline cartilage (type II collagen) and degrades over time.
items.note: Classic subspecialty question on cartilage repair tissue composition following marrow stimulation.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes Type A synoviocytes located in the intimal layer of the synovial membrane?
o: They are mesenchymal fibroblast-like cells that produce hyaluronic acid and lubricin.
They form tight junctions sitting on a continuous basement membrane.
They secrete large amounts of fibrinogen into normal non-inflammatory synovial fluid.
They are bone marrow-derived cells of monocyte lineage that perform phagocytic functions.
items.e: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like cells derived from bone marrow monocytes (expressing CD68) that function in phagocytosis and antigen presentation. Type B synoviocytes are fibroblast-like mesenchymal cells that synthesize hyaluronic acid and lubricin.
items.note: Standard Basic Sciences question testing synoviocyte classification and function.

items.q: A 58-year-old man presents with acute knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis shows cloudy yellow fluid with a WBC count of 38,000/mm³. Polarised light microscopy reveals weakly positive, blue birefringent, rod- and rhomboid-shaped crystals when aligned parallel to the compensator axis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals are rhomboid or rod-shaped with weak positive birefringence (appearing blue when parallel to the red compensator axis). Monosodium urate crystals in gout are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel).
items.note: High-yield synovial fluid microscopy question with unambiguous optical features.

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage contains round chondrocytes arranged in vertical columns, collagen fibrils oriented perpendicular to the surface, the highest proteoglycan content, and the lowest water content?
items.e: The deep (radial) zone makes up about 30% of articular cartilage and features round chondrocytes in vertical columns with perpendicular collagen fibrils. It contains the highest proteoglycan content and lowest water content to resist compressive forces.
items.note: Factually accurate and tests structural zonal anatomy of articular cartilage.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent atraumatic bloody knee effusions. Gradient-echo MRI demonstrates nodular synovial masses with low signal intensity on T1 and T2 images and prominent 'blooming' artifact. Cytogenetics reveals a translocation causing CSF1 overexpression. What is the diagnosis?
o: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (Pigmented villonodular synovitis)
items.e: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS) is driven by a CSF1 gene translocation that overexpresses CSF1. Haemosiderin accumulation from recurrent haemorrhagic effusions produces characteristic low T1/T2 MRI signals with blooming artifacts on gradient-echo sequences.
items.note: Excellent clinical-pathological correlation question testing PVNS genetics and MRI hallmamrks.

items.q: During dynamic joint motion under high cyclic loading, which mode of fluid-film lubrication is considered the primary mechanism preventing direct cartilage contact by generating fluid pressurisation as cartilage deforms?
o: Boundary lubrication mediated by hyaluronic acid
items.e: Elastohydrodynamic lubrication is the main mode of fluid-film lubrication during dynamic joint motion. The deformable nature of articular cartilage increases contact area under load and traps a pressurized fluid film between moving joint surfaces.
items.note: Standard tribology/biomechanics question with clear options.

items.q: Specific catabolic enzymes drive cartilage matrix degradation in osteoarthritis. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for the enzymatic cleavage and breakdown of Type II collagen fibrils?
items.e: MMP-13 (collagenase-3) is the principal matrix metalloproteinase responsible for degrading type II collagen fibrils in articular cartilage. ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5 are aggrecanases that specifically cleave aggrecan proteoglycans.
items.note: High-yield cartilage degradation enzymology question frequently asked in entrance exams.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with symptomatic right hip osteoarthritis is advised on non-operative management strategies to decrease hip joint reaction forces during walking. Which of the following recommendations is biomechanically correct?
o: Hold a walking cane in the ipsilateral (right) hand
Hold a walking cane in the contralateral (left) hand
Carry heavy grocery bags in the contralateral (left) hand
Lean the torso toward the contralateral side during stance phase
items.e: Holding a walking cane in the contralateral hand provides a long lever arm relative to the hip joint, reducing the required abductor muscle force and decreasing joint reaction force by up to 40–60%. Conversely, carrying loads in the contralateral hand increases joint reaction force, while holding loads in the ipsilateral hand reduces it.
items.note: Accurate biomechanical concept, clear options, well-supported by reference notes.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon is assembling a monoplanar external fixator for an unstable open tibial shaft fracture. To achieve the single most effective increase in construct bending stiffness, which modification should be implemented?
o: Increase the diameter of the Schanz pins
Place the connecting bar further away from the bone
Decrease the distance between the two pins within the proximal fragment
items.e: Increasing pin diameter provides the greatest increase in external fixator stiffness because bending stiffness is proportional to the pin radius to the fourth power (r^4). Placing the connecting bar closer to bone and spreading pins wider apart within each fragment also increase stiffness.
items.note: High-yield standard question on external fixator biomechanics, mathematically and clinically accurate.

items.q: According to Perren's strain theory, what interfragmentary strain environment is required to stimulate secondary (indirect) bone healing with callus formation?
items.e: Interfragmentary strain between 2% and 10% promotes secondary (indirect) bone healing with callus under conditions of relative stability. Strain under 2% leads to primary bone healing, whereas strain exceeding 10% results in non-union and tissue breakdown.
items.note: Classic exam question on Perren's strain theory, fully accurate and standard.

items.q: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) bone cement is supplied as a powder and a liquid monomer component. Which substance is included in the liquid monomer to act as a stabilizer/inhibitor to prevent premature polymerisation during storage?
items.e: Hydroquinone is added to the liquid MMA monomer as a stabilizer/inhibitor to prevent premature self-polymerisation. Benzoyl peroxide is the initiator in the powder component, DMPT is the accelerator in the liquid, and barium sulfate is a radiopacifier in the powder.
items.note: High-yield biomaterials question with accurate distractors.

items.q: Stress shielding around joint replacements occurs when load is preferentially borne by a stiff implant rather than host bone. Which metallic biomaterial has a Young's modulus of elasticity closest to that of cortical bone (~15–20 GPa)?
items.e: Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) has a Young's modulus of elasticity of approximately 110 GPa, which is the lowest among common implant metals and closest to cortical bone (15–20 GPa), thereby reducing stress shielding. Stainless steel (~190–200 GPa), Cobalt-chromium (~210–230 GPa), and Alumina (~350–400 GPa) are substantially stiffer.
items.note: Standard biomaterial modulus comparison question, fully correct.

items.q: During the processing of highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE) for total hip arthroplasty, thermal treatment above the melting point (remelting) is performed after irradiation. What is the primary mechanical disadvantage of remelting?
o: Reduces fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength of the material
Leaves abundant residual free radicals causing rapid oxidation and delamination
Increases adhesive and abrasive wear rates compared to conventional non-irradiated polyethylene
Triggers an acute cytotoxic immune response upon joint implantation
items.e: Remelting HXLPE above its melting point eliminates residual free radicals (preventing oxidation), but it alters the crystalline structure, thereby reducing mechanical properties such as fatigue strength, toughness, and yield strength. Annealing below the melting point preserves strength but leaves residual free radicals.
items.note: Accurate depiction of HXLPE processing trade-offs commonly tested in SS exams.

items.q: A 70-year-old male with a total hip arthroplasty (modular CoCr femoral head on a titanium alloy stem) presents with hip discomfort. Diagnostic workup reveals mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC / trunnionosis) at the head-neck taper. Which serum ion pattern is classic for this condition?
o: Isolated elevation of serum titanium ions only
Serum cobalt elevation significantly greater than serum chromium elevation
Serum chromium elevation significantly greater than serum cobalt elevation
Equal elevation of serum nickel and iron ions with normal cobalt
items.e: Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC / trunnionosis) at a modular taper interface (CoCr head on Ti stem) characteristically causes preferential release of cobalt into the circulation, resulting in elevated serum cobalt levels that are significantly higher than serum chromium levels.
items.note: Factually accurate and classic question on trunnionosis ion patterns.

items.q: When performing a biopsy of a long bone tumor, creating an open-section longitudinal rectangular cortical window drastically reduces structural strength. Which loading mode suffers the most severe reduction in strength (up to 90%) from an open-section defect?
items.e: An open-section defect (a longitudinal cortical slot or window) severely impairs the bone's cross-sectional geometry and polar moment of inertia, reducing torsional strength by up to 90%. For this reason, biopsy defects should ideally be round or oval with rounded margins to limit stress concentration.
items.note: Standard bone biomechanics question on stress risers and open-section defects.

items.q: Which connective tissue layer of a peripheral nerve contains tight junctions forming the blood-nerve barrier and provides the primary source of tensile strength of the nerve?
items.e: The perineurium surrounds individual nerve fascicles and contains tight junctions that constitute the blood-nerve barrier. It is the primary contributor to the tensile strength of a peripheral nerve and maintains intrafascicular pressure.
items.note: Accurate, classic exam question with unambiguous options directly matching high-yield reference notes.

items.q: A patient undergoing a peripheral regional block experiences progressive, sequential loss of neurological function as local anaesthetic diffuses into the nerve. Which of the following functions is lost FIRST?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block smaller-diameter nerve fibres before larger ones. Unmyelinated or thin B (autonomic) fibres are blocked first, followed by A-delta/C (pain and temperature), A-beta (touch/pressure), and lastly thick A-alpha (motor and proprioception) fibres.
items.note: Directly supported by the Erlanger-Gasser classification principles and pharmacological block sequence.

items.q: A 22-year-old motorcyclist sustains a traction injury to the brachial plexus, causing complete sensory loss in the C6 dermatome. Electrodiagnostic testing at 4 weeks post-injury shows a completely preserved sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) amplitude for the superficial radial nerve. Where is the lesion located?
o: Preganglionic root avulsion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
Upper trunk distal to the dorsal root ganglion
items.e: In a preganglionic (root avulsion) injury, the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) and sensory cell bodies remain intact and attached to the peripheral axon. Consequently, distal sensory axonal degeneration does not occur, leaving the SNAP preserved despite complete clinical anaesthesia in the dermatome.
items.note: High-yield electrodiagnostic topic for SS exams; completely accurate and standard rationale.

items.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a closed midshaft humeral fracture and an complete radial nerve palsy. Closed reduction and functional bracing are performed. What is the most appropriate initial management for the nerve injury?
o: Immediate operative exploration and primary nerve repair
Electromyography (EMG) on post-injury day 1 to assess axonal disruption
Clinical observation with serial examination and electrodiagnosis at 3 to 4 weeks
Operative exploration and sural nerve autografting at 2 weeks
items.e: Closed injuries associated with nerve palsies are predominantly neurapraxias or axonotmeses, with high spontaneous recovery rates (70-90% for radial palsy in closed humerus fractures). Initial observation is indicated, with EMG delayed to 3-4 weeks to accurately distinguish neurapraxia from axonal loss.
items.note: Standard orthopaedic principle supported by Campbell's and exam standards.

items.q: During active concentric muscle contraction, which region of the sarcomere remains constant in length according to the sliding filament theory?
items.e: The A band represents the entire length of the thick myosin filaments and maintains a constant length during contraction. The I band (actin only) and H zone (myosin only) shorten as thin filaments slide past thick filaments, bringing adjacent Z lines closer.
items.note: Basic muscle physiology core question; factually flawless.

items.q: A 16-year-old male undergoing open reduction of a femur fracture under general anaesthesia develops a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, generalized muscle rigidity, and severe tachycardia. What is the underlying pathophysiology of this condition?
o: Autoantibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
Antibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum due to an RYR1 receptor gene mutation
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in the RYR1 gene (ryanodine receptor), leading to uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when exposed to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine. A rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 is the earliest clinical sign.
items.note: High-yield neuromuscular junction and pathology topic; accurate stem and options.

items.q: In accordance with Henneman's size principle, which motor units are recruited first during a gradually increasing voluntary isometric muscle contraction?
o: Large motor units containing Type IIB fast glycolytic fibres
Small motor units containing Type I slow oxidative fibres
Intermediate motor units containing Type IIA fast oxidative-glycolytic fibres
Large motor units containing Type IIA fibres
items.e: Henneman's size principle dictates that smaller motor units containing Type I (slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant) muscle fibres are recruited first at low force levels, while larger motor units containing Type II fibres are progressively recruited as force requirements increase.
items.note: Standard basic science core concept; cleanly written.

items.q: An athlete sustains a severe direct contusion to the anterior thigh during a sporting event. To minimize knee stiffness and decrease the time required to return to competition, how should the knee be positioned during the initial 24 hours of immobilization?
items.e: Immobilizing the knee in approximately 120 degrees of flexion for the first 24 hours following an acute quadriceps contusion limits deep haematoma formation, preserves knee motion, and significantly reduces stiffness and return-to-play duration.
items.note: Classic sports/muscle injury exam fact straight from Campbell's and standard guidelines.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon conducts a prospective study following two cohorts of patients: one group treated with an intramedullary nail and another with a locking plate for proximal humerus fractures. Patients are followed for 2 years to assess nonunion rates. According to the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (JBJS) levels of evidence for therapeutic studies, what level of evidence does this study represent?
items.e: Prospective comparative (cohort) studies represent Level II evidence according to the JBJS hierarchy for therapeutic studies. In contrast, retrospective comparative cohort studies and case-control studies are classified as Level III, whereas high-quality RCTs represent Level I.
items.note: Accurate assessment of JBJS level of evidence for prospective cohort studies.

items.q: A research group evaluates functional recovery using the Oxford Knee Score before surgery and at 1-year follow-up in 30 patients undergoing total knee replacement. The score distribution is non-normally distributed (skewed). Which statistical test is most appropriate to evaluate if there is a significant change in scores postoperatively?
items.e: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric equivalent of the paired t-test, used for comparing two paired or related measurements when data are skewed or ordinal. The Mann-Whitney U test is used for comparing two independent non-parametric groups.
items.note: Correct statistical test choice for paired non-parametric data.

items.q: Which of the following reporting guidelines should be followed when preparing a manuscript for a systematic review and meta-analysis of orthopaedic interventions?
items.e: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is the standard reporting guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. CONSORT is used for randomised controlled trials, STROBE for observational studies, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies.
items.note: Fully supported standard reporting guideline definition.

items.q: A diagnostic blood test for prosthetic joint infection has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. If this test is applied in a tertiary revision unit with a high disease prevalence rather than a community setting with a low disease prevalence, how will the test statistics behave?
o: Sensitivity increases and Positive Predictive Value (PPV) decreases
Sensitivity and Specificity remain unchanged, while PPV increases
Specificity increases and Negative Predictive Value (NPV) increases
Both PPV and NPV will increase simultaneously
items.e: Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios are intrinsic properties of a test and do not change with disease prevalence. Predictive values depend heavily on prevalence: as prevalence rises, the Positive Predictive Value (PPV) increases and the Negative Predictive Value (NPV) decreases.
items.note: Factually flawless question on diagnostic test statistics and prevalence.

items.q: In a randomised controlled trial comparing two surgical techniques for distal radius fractures, which design feature is specifically effective at controlling for both known and unknown confounding variables at baseline?
items.e: Randomisation is the only methodological technique that balances both known and unknown confounding variables between groups at baseline. Allocation concealment prevents selection bias, whereas blinding prevents performance and detection bias.
items.note: Core methodological concept correctly tested.

items.q: A trial reports that a novel wound dressing reduces the risk of surgical site infection after total joint arthroplasty from 10% in the control group to 5% in the intervention group. What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) to prevent one surgical site infection?
items.e: The Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) is calculated as Control Event Rate (10%) minus Experimental Event Rate (5%), which equals 5% (0.05). The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.05 = 20.
items.note: Standard statistical calculation, clear and correct.

items.q: When conducting a long-term survivorship analysis of joint replacement implants in an elderly population, patient death acts as a competing risk. If standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis is used without accounting for competing risks, what is the impact on the reported revision rate?
o: It underestimates the cumulative revision rate
It overestimates the cumulative revision rate
It has no effect on the revision rate estimate
It invalidates the log-rank test p-value
items.e: In survival analysis of elderly cohorts, death prevents the occurrence of implant revision (competing risk). Standard Kaplan-Meier analysis treats dead patients as censored, which artificially overestimates the cumulative revision rate over time; the Cumulative Incidence Function (Fine and Gray method) should be used instead.
items.note: High-yield statistical concept specific to joint registry and survival analyses.

items.q: A surgeon is performing intraoperative fluoroscopy for distal locking of a femoral intramedullary nail. Which of the following technical setups will minimise radiation exposure to both the patient and operating room staff?
o: Place the X-ray tube above the table and the image intensifier below
Position the image intensifier as close to the patient as possible
Stand on the X-ray tube side of the patient when acquiring lateral views
Routine use of magnification (zoom) mode to lower tube voltage output
items.e: To minimise scatter and patient dose, the image intensifier should be placed close to the patient while keeping the X-ray tube as far away as possible under the operating table. Scatter is highest on the tube side, so staff should stand on the intensifier side, and magnification modes increase dose.
items.note: Accurate, standard intraoperative fluoroscopy safety question supported by reference notes.

items.q: According to current International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) recommendations, what is the annual occupational equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye in a radiation worker?
o: 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
items.e: The ICRP annual limit for the lens of the eye for occupational workers is 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (with no single year exceeding 50 mSv). The limit for skin, hands, and feet is 500 mSv per year, and for the general public, it is 1 mSv per year.
items.note: Factually precise question on ICRP occupational dose limits.

items.q: A patient undergoes computed tomography (CT) for a complex intra-articular fracture. When assessing tissue attenuation values on the scan, which pairing of tissue to Hounsfield Units (HU) is correct?
items.e: Acute blood measures approximately +50 to +80 HU on CT. Water is defined as 0 HU, air is -1000 HU, fat is -100 to -50 HU, and cortical bone measures +1000 HU or more.
items.note: Standard attenuation value question with clear correct pairing and unambiguous distractors.

items.q: A 35-year-old tennis player undergoes MRI of the shoulder. Signal hyperintensity is noted in the supraspinatus tendon on short-TE (T1 and proton density) sequences, which completely disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences. What artefact explains this non-pathologic finding?
items.e: The magic angle effect occurs when collagen fibres are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the main magnetic field (B0), resulting in increased signal intensity on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE) that disappears on long-TE (T2-weighted) sequences.
items.note: Classic MSK MRI artifact question with exact clinical vignette characteristics.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman undergoes Dual-energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) for osteoporosis evaluation. Which of the following factors is most likely to produce a falsely high areal bone mineral density (BMD) reading at the lumbar spine?
items.e: Degenerative osteophytes, facet joint arthritis, aortic calcification, and vertebral compression fractures add extra mineralised tissue in the 2D projection path of DEXA, causing a falsely elevated lumbar spine BMD.
items.note: High-yield DEXA pitfall question matching textbook teaching.

items.q: A Tc-99m methylene diphosphonate (MDP) triple-phase radionuclide bone scan is requested for diagnostic workup. Which of the following skeletal conditions typically manifests as a 'cold' (photopenic) lesion on the delayed phase?
items.e: Multiple myeloma produces purely lytic lesions with minimal or no osteoblastic activity, typically appearing photopenic or 'cold' on a Tc-99m MDP bone scan. Osteoid osteoma, Paget disease, and CRPS characteristically demonstrate increased ('hot') radionuclide uptake.
items.note: Standard nuclear medicine question distinguishing hot vs cold bone scan lesions.

items.q: During musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of the Achilles tendon, an image artefact causes a normal tendon structure to appear falsely hypoechoic when the transducer beam strikes the tissue at a non-perpendicular angle. What is this artefact called?
items.e: Anisotropy occurs in linear fibrillar structures like tendons and ligaments when the ultrasound beam is not perpendicular (90 degrees) to the fibres, leading to a false hypoechoic appearance mimicking a tear or tendinopathy.
items.note: Fundamental MSK ultrasound artifact question.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding X-ray physics and interactions with biological tissue is correct?
o: Approximately 99% of electron kinetic energy at the anode target is converted into heat, with only about 1% converted into X-rays
Increasing peak kilovoltage (kVp) increases image contrast by enhancing the photoelectric effect
Compton scatter is the dominant interaction producing contrast at low photon energies in high atomic number tissue like bone
Aluminium filtration is used in the tube assembly to absorb high-energy photons to protect the digital detector
items.e: In an X-ray tube, about 99% of kinetic energy is converted into heat at the tungsten anode, with only ~1% converted to X-rays. Increasing kVp increases penetration and scatter while decreasing contrast; the photoelectric effect dominates at low energies in high atomic number tissues, and filtration removes low-energy photons to lower patient skin dose.
items.note: Accurate basic radiation physics question with distinct, unambiguous options.

items.q: A 75-year-old patient scheduled for semi-elective hip fracture surgery had an acute myocardial infarction 6 weeks prior to presentation. According to the ASA physical status classification system, which class best describes this patient?
items.e: An acute myocardial infarction within the preceding 3 months is categorized as ASA IV (severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life). ASA III represents severe systemic disease without a constant threat to life, while ASA V represents a moribund patient.
items.note: Accurate, standard ASA classification item directly supported by reference notes.

items.q: A 65-year-old patient undergoing revision total hip arthroplasty for chronic staphylococcal prosthetic joint infection is prescribed oral rifampicin for its biofilm-clearing property. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Direct inhibition of bacterial RNA polymerase
items.e: Rifampicin acts by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and is uniquely active against staphylococcal biofilm in implant infections. It must never be used as monotherapy due to rapid emergence of resistance.
items.note: Factually correct, clear pharmacology question fully supported by text.

items.q: During closed reduction of a distal radius fracture under intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block), which local anaesthetic agent is strictly contraindicated due to severe cardiotoxicity?
items.e: Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic agent and is strictly contraindicated for intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier block). Prilocaine is the agent of choice for Bier block, while lidocaine is also used.
items.note: High-yield, standard orthopaedic pharmacology fact supported by notes.

items.q: A 72-year-old postmenopausal female with severe osteoporosis is being evaluated for osteoanabolic treatment. She sustained an ischemic stroke 8 months ago. Which medication is contraindicated due to an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events?
items.e: Romosozumab is a monoclonal antibody against sclerostin with dual anabolic and antiresorptive action; results from the ARCH trial showed an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events, leading to a warning against its use in patients with a myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year.
items.note: Well-constructed question on bone-active agents supported by the guidelines in the notes.

items.q: A 68-year-old male receiving prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) following total knee arthroplasty exhibits a 60% drop in platelet count on postoperative day 7, along with a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
o: Switch LMWH to therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion
Discontinue LMWH and initiate argatroban or fondaparinux
Transfuse pooled random donor platelets immediately
Discontinue LMWH and immediately start oral warfarin loading
items.e: This clinical picture represents Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT Type II). Management requires stopping all heparin products immediately and initiating a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux; platelet transfusions and starting warfarin prior to platelet recovery are contraindicated.
items.note: Clear clinical scenario testing HIT management, completely supported by notes.

items.q: According to the ACR/AAHKS guidelines for elective total joint arthroplasty in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, which medication should be CONTINUED uninterrupted through the perioperative period?
items.e: Current ACR/AAHKS perioperative guidelines recommend continuing conventional synthetic DMARDs like methotrexate, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine, and sulfasalazine. Biologic agents (e.g., adalimumab) should be withheld until the end of their dosing cycle, and JAK inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib, upadacitinib) should be stopped 3 days before surgery.
items.note: Accurate guideline-based question fully supported by notes.

items.q: During elective posterior spinal instrumentation under general anaesthesia with volatile anaesthetic agents, what is the EARLIEST clinical sign of malignant hyperthermia?
items.e: The earliest manifestation of malignant hyperthermia is an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 (capnography elevation), often accompanied by sinus tachycardia and masseter spasm. Hyperthermia is a late sign of the disorder.
items.note: Classic intraoperative emergency question supported by reference notes.

items.q: During cement insertion for a hemiarthroplasty, an 84-year-old female experiences a fall in systolic blood pressure from 130 mmHg to 70 mmHg (SBP drop > 40%) along with an oxygen saturation drop to 85%. According to the Donaldson classification, which grade of Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS) is present?
items.e: Donaldson Grade 2 BCIS is defined by severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%), severe hypotension (systolic blood pressure fall > 40%), or unexpected loss of consciousness. Grade 1 involves moderate hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) or hypotension (20–40% fall), while Grade 3 involves cardiac collapse requiring CPR.
items.note: Factually accurate question testing BCIS grading supported directly by the notes.

items.q: Which of the following ligaments is the strongest in the human body and serves as the primary determinant of posterior pelvic ring stability?
items.e: The posterior sacroiliac ligaments are the strongest ligaments in the body and are the most important components for maintaining the stability of the posterior pelvic ring.
items.note: Directly supported by the reference notes regarding pelvic anatomy and ligamentous strength.

items.q: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-energy motor vehicle accident. He has a clinically unstable pelvis. If the patient has arterial bleeding from the posterior pelvic complex, which vessel is most likely involved?
items.e: While 80-90% of pelvic bleeding is venous, the superior gluteal artery (branch of the internal iliac) is the most common arterial source of bleeding, especially in posterior ring disruptions.
items.note: Matches the reference notes regarding arterial bleeding sources in pelvic trauma.

items.q: In the radiographic evaluation of a pelvic ring injury, which specific view is most diagnostic for assessing vertical displacement (migration) of a hemipelvis?
items.e: The pelvic outlet view, taken with the beam angled 40-45 degrees cephalad, is the best view to demonstrate vertical displacement and sacral foraminal anatomy.
items.note: Correctly identifies the utility of the outlet view as per the reference notes.

items.q: According to the Young-Burgess classification, which of the following injury patterns is associated with the highest volume of blood loss and the greatest requirement for emergency blood transfusions?
items.e: APC III injuries involve complete disruption of the anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, leading to the highest risk of massive hemorrhage and transfusion requirements.
items.note: Matches the clinical associations of the Young-Burgess classification provided in the notes.

items.q: A patient sustains a sacral fracture that passes medial to the sacral foramina, involving the central spinal canal. According to the Denis classification, what is the most likely clinical finding associated with this injury zone?
items.e: Denis Zone III fractures involve the central sacral canal and carry a high risk (approx. 57%) of neurological deficit, specifically bowel, bladder, and sexual dysfunction.
items.note: Accurately reflects the Denis classification and associated neurological risks.

items.q: In the radiographic assessment of acetabular fractures using Judet views, the obturator oblique view is specifically used to visualize the:
items.e: The obturator oblique view (45-degree oblique) provides the best visualization of the anterior column and the posterior wall of the acetabulum.
items.note: Correctly identifies the structures seen on Judet views as per the reference notes.

items.q: During the evaluation of a complex acetabular fracture, the presence of a 'spur sign' on the obturator oblique radiograph indicates that the fracture is a:
items.e: The spur sign represents the posterior-superior ilium which is no longer attached to the articular surface; it is pathognomonic for a both-column fracture.
items.note: Correctly identifies the pathognomonic sign for both-column fractures.

items.q: A 28-year-old female sustains a posterior hip dislocation. Post-reduction CT reveals a femoral head fracture located cephalad to the fovea capitis (weight-bearing portion) and an associated femoral neck fracture. This is classified as a Pipkin Type:
items.e: Pipkin Type III fractures involve a femoral head fracture (Type I or II) associated with a concomitant femoral neck fracture; this pattern has the worst prognosis.
items.note: Correctly applies the Pipkin classification based on the injury description.

items.q: A 76-year-old active female sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture (Garden IV). According to the HEALTH trial and NICE guidelines, which management plan is most appropriate for a patient who is medically fit and walks independently outdoors?
items.e: For active, independent, and cognitively intact elderly patients with displaced neck fractures, total hip arthroplasty (THA) is recommended over hemiarthroplasty for better functional outcomes. The WHiTE 5 trial supports using cemented stems to reduce pain and periprosthetic fracture risk.
items.note: The question accurately reflects current guidelines (NICE) and major trial evidence (HEALTH, WHiTE 5) for the management of displaced neck fractures in the elderly.

items.q: Regarding the blood supply to the adult femoral head, which of the following statements is correct based on the applied anatomy of the proximal femur?
o: The artery of the ligamentum teres provides the majority of the blood supply in adults.
The lateral femoral circumflex artery is the primary source via its posterosuperior branches.
The lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery provide the main supply.
Intracapsular fractures rarely disrupt the retinacular vessels due to their protected location.
items.e: The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), specifically its lateral epiphyseal (retinacular) branches running up the posterosuperior neck, is the primary blood supply to the femoral head. Intracapsular fractures often disrupt these vessels, leading to high rates of AVN.
items.note: This is a fundamental anatomical fact in orthopaedic trauma, correctly identifying the MFCA as the primary source.

items.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a vertical femoral neck fracture following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. The fracture line is oriented at 65 degrees from the horizontal. Which of the following is true regarding this injury?
o: It is a Pauwels Type I fracture with a low risk of non-union.
It represents a Pauwels Type III fracture, which carries the highest risk of vertical shear and fixation failure.
Primary treatment should be a cemented hemiarthroplasty within 48 hours.
The fracture is considered stable and can be managed with protected weight bearing.
items.e: A fracture angle >50 degrees from the horizontal is classified as Pauwels Type III. This represents a vertical shear pattern with the highest risk of non-union and fixation failure in young patients, necessitating urgent anatomical reduction and stable fixation.
items.note: The question correctly applies the Pauwels classification and the management principles for young patients with high-energy neck fractures.

items.q: In the management of intertrochanteric fractures, which fracture characteristic is considered a contraindication for the use of a sliding (dynamic) hip screw (DHS)?
o: Presence of a simple two-part A1.1 pattern
Intact lateral wall thicker than 25 mm
Posteromedial comminution limited to the lesser trochanter
items.e: The DHS is contraindicated in reverse obliquity fractures because the fracture line allows the femoral shaft to slide medially along the lag screw axis, leading to failure. Cephalomedullary nails are the treatment of choice for these unstable patterns.
items.note: The contraindication of DHS in reverse obliquity patterns is a high-yield, standard orthopaedic principle.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient on long-term bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis presents with prodromal thigh pain. Radiographs reveal a transverse, non-comminuted subtrochanteric fracture with a distinct lateral cortical 'beaking'. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Increase the dose of bisphosphonates and prescribe bed rest
Perform a total hip arthroplasty with a long uncemented stem
Stop bisphosphonates, consider teriparatide, and proceed with intramedullary nailing
Apply a hip spica cast for 12 weeks to allow secondary bone healing
items.e: These are features of an Atypical Femoral Fracture (AFF). Management includes stopping the bisphosphonate, supplementing with Vitamin D/Calcium, considering teriparatide to stimulate bone healing, and surgical fixation (usually an intramedullary nail).
items.note: The question correctly identifies the clinical presentation and multi-modal management of atypical femoral fractures.

items.q: During the surgical fixation of a subtrochanteric fracture, the surgeon notes that the proximal fragment is flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. Which muscle is primarily responsible for the flexion deformity of this fragment?
items.e: In subtrochanteric fractures, the proximal fragment is deformed by the iliopsoas (flexion), gluteus medius/minimus (abduction), and short external rotators (external rotation). The distal fragment is typically adducted by the adductors.
items.note: The deforming forces in subtrochanteric fractures are classic anatomy-based exam questions.

items.q: Which of the following is considered a 'Major' criterion in the Gurd and Wilson classification for the diagnosis of Fat Embolism Syndrome following a femoral shaft fracture?
o: Petechial rash in the axilla or conjunctiva
items.e: Gurd and Wilson's major criteria for Fat Embolism Syndrome include respiratory insufficiency, cerebral signs (not explained by other causes), and a petechial rash (typically found in the axilla, neck, or conjunctiva). Tachycardia and pyrexia are minor criteria.
items.note: The Gurd and Wilson criteria are the standard for diagnosing Fat Embolism Syndrome in orthopaedic trauma.

items.q: To minimize the risk of 'cut-out' when fixing an intertrochanteric fracture with a lag screw, what is the recommended Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) according to Baumgaertner?
items.e: The Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) is the sum of the distance from the tip of the lag screw to the apex of the femoral head on both AP and lateral views. A TAD of less than 25 mm is the strongest predictor of preventing mechanical cut-out.
items.note: TAD is a universally accepted surgical parameter in the fixation of extracapsular hip fractures.

items.q: A 42-year-old male presents with a valgus-load injury to the knee. Radiographs reveal a split of the lateral tibial plateau accompanied by a central articular depression. According to the Schatzker classification, which type is this, and what is its clinical significance?
o: Type I; most common in osteoporotic bone
Type II; most common tibial plateau fracture pattern
Type III; associated with the highest risk of compartment syndrome
Type IV; often involves a fracture-dislocation mechanism
items.e: Schatzker Type II is a lateral split-depression fracture and is the most common tibial plateau fracture pattern. Type III is typically seen in osteoporotic bone, while Type IV and VI carry higher risks of neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome respectively.
items.note: The question accurately identifies the most common fracture pattern and correctly matches the description to the Schatzker classification.

items.q: A patient with a high-energy Schatzker Type VI tibial plateau fracture is being evaluated in the emergency department. The leg is grossly swollen. The Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) is measured at 0.85. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Application of a long leg cast and elevation
Four-compartment fasciotomy based on ABI alone
items.e: According to the source notes, an Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) of less than 0.9 in high-energy tibial plateau fractures (especially Schatzker IV and VI) necessitates an arterial study to rule out popliteal artery injury.
items.note: The question correctly uses the ABI threshold of 0.9 for vascular evaluation in high-energy knee trauma as per standard protocols.

items.q: Which of the following soft tissue injuries is most frequently associated with lateral tibial plateau fractures?
items.e: Lateral meniscus tears are the most common associated soft-tissue injury in lateral tibial plateau fractures; these tears are often peripheral and can sometimes become incarcerated within the fracture site.
items.note: The fact is well-supported by Campbell's and the provided notes as the most common associated injury.

items.q: An 80-year-old female with known osteoporosis sustains a low-energy fall. Radiographs show a pure depression of the lateral tibial plateau without an associated split or wedge fragment. What is the classification and recommended surgical technique?
o: Schatzker II; lateral buttress plating only
Schatzker III; elevation through a cortical window and subchondral grafting
items.e: Schatzker Type III is a pure lateral depression fracture typically seen in elderly, osteoporotic patients. Treatment involves elevating the depressed articular surface through a cortical window and supporting it with bone graft or substitute and raft screws.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the fracture type and the specific surgical technique (cortical window/rafting) required for pure depression fractures.

items.q: A 35-year-old patient sustains a high-energy pilon fracture. The surgeon decides to follow the staged protocol. What is the primary goal of the first stage of management?
o: Definitive fixation of the tibial plafond to allow early range of motion
Application of a spanning external fixator to restore length and alignment via ligamentotaxis
Primary ankle arthrodesis to prevent post-traumatic arthritis
Immediate bone grafting of the metaphyseal defect
items.e: The staged protocol for pilon fractures begins with an urgent spanning external fixator to restore length, alignment, and rotation through ligamentotaxis, allowing soft tissues to settle before definitive ORIF.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the standard of care for high-energy pilon fractures.

items.q: In the classic four-step reconstruction of a pilon fracture described by Rüedi and Allgöwer, which step is performed first?
o: Reconstruction of the distal tibial articular surface
items.e: The Rüedi-Allgöwer principles for pilon ORIF follow a specific sequence: (1) restore fibular length, (2) reconstruct the articular surface, (3) bone graft the metaphyseal defect, and (4) buttress the medial tibia.
items.note: This is a classic orthopedic principle frequently tested in exams.

items.q: A CT scan of a complex tibial plateau fracture shows a large shear fragment in the posteromedial column. Which surgical approach is specifically indicated to address and buttress this fragment?
