items.e: The three-column concept identifies posterior column fragments (especially posteromedial) that are often missed by Schatzker classification. These require a posteromedial approach (such as the Lobenhoffer) for direct visualization and buttress plating.
items.note: The question tests the modern three-column concept and the corresponding surgical approach, which is a high-yield topic.

items.q: During the ORIF of a pilon fracture, the surgeon identifies the anterolateral articular fragment that is attached to the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL). This is known as the:
items.e: The Chaput fragment is the anterolateral fragment of the distal tibia attached to the AITFL. The Volkmann fragment is the posterolateral fragment attached to the PITFL.
items.note: The question correctly tests eponyms associated with pilon and ankle fracture fragments.

items.q: A 32-year-old male presents with a trimalleolar fracture. Intraoperatively, the surgeon notes a residual lateral talar shift of 1 mm after fibular fixation. According to the classic study by Ramsey and Hamilton, this residual shift reduces the tibiotalar contact area by approximately:
items.e: Ramsey and Hamilton demonstrated that just 1 mm of lateral talar shift results in a 42% reduction in the contact area of the tibiotalar joint, which provides the biomechanical basis for the requirement of anatomical reduction.
items.note: Classic, high-yield biomechanical fact supported by the reference notes and standard textbooks.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman sustains an ankle injury after a fall. Radiographs reveal a short oblique fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis, running from anteroinferior to posterosuperior. According to the Lauge-Hansen classification, which of the following represents the correct sequence of injury for this pattern?
o: I: Medial malleolus fracture -> II: AITFL rupture -> III: Fibula fracture -> IV: PITFL rupture
I: AITFL rupture -> II: Spiral fibula fracture -> III: PITFL or posterior malleolus fracture -> IV: Medial malleolus fracture/deltoid rupture
I: AITFL rupture -> II: PITFL rupture -> III: Fibula fracture -> IV: Medial malleolus fracture
I: Medial malleolus fracture -> II: Fibula fracture -> III: AITFL rupture -> IV: PITFL rupture
items.e: This describes a Supination-External Rotation (SER) injury (Weber B). The sequence is Stage I: AITFL; Stage II: short oblique/spiral fibula at the level of the syndesmosis; Stage III: PITFL or posterior malleolus; Stage IV: medial malleolus fracture or deltoid rupture.
items.note: Accurately tests the most common Lauge-Hansen pattern and its sequence as per the reference notes.

items.q: A patient presents with a Weber A fibular avulsion fracture and a vertical fracture of the medial malleolus with associated impaction of the medial tibial plafond. Which Lauge-Hansen mechanism is most likely responsible for this injury pattern?
items.e: Supination-Adduction (SAD) injuries typically result in a transverse fibular avulsion (Weber A) in Stage I, followed by a vertical medial malleolus fracture and medial plafond impaction in Stage II.
items.note: Correctly identifies the SAD pattern, which is unique for its vertical medial malleolus fracture and plafond impaction.

items.q: On an AP radiograph of the ankle, which of the following measurements, taken 1 cm above the tibial plafond, is considered the most reliable radiographic indicator of a syndesmotic injury?
items.e: While multiple measurements exist, the tibiofibular clear space (measured on the AP view, 1 cm above the plafond) being over 5-6 mm is considered the most reliable radiographic indicator of syndesmotic injury.
items.note: Tests a specific, high-yield radiographic threshold mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A 28-year-old athlete sustains a trimalleolar fracture. CT shows a posterolateral oblique fragment involving 30% of the articular surface with associated posterior talar subluxation. Which of the following is the preferred management for the posterior malleolar fragment according to current evidence?
o: Indirect reduction and fixation with an anterior-to-posterior screw
Direct fixation via a posterolateral approach
Conservative management as it will reduce automatically with the fibula
items.e: Current evidence favors direct fixation of larger posterior malleolar fragments (over 25-30% or with subluxation) via a posterolateral approach, as it restores syndesmotic stability and incisura congruity better than indirect methods.
items.note: Reflects modern orthopaedic practice and the specific recommendations in the reference notes.

items.q: A 50-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with an ankle fracture-dislocation. Despite multiple attempts, closed reduction is unsuccessful. Radiographs show the proximal fibular fragment trapped behind the posterolateral tibia in the incisura. This injury is known as:
items.e: A Bosworth fracture-dislocation occurs when the fibula is trapped behind the posterior tibial tubercle (incisura). It is irreducible by closed means and represents a surgical emergency for open reduction.
items.note: Tests a classic eponym and its clinical significance (irreducibility).

items.q: A 62-year-old diabetic patient with peripheral neuropathy sustains an unstable bimalleolar ankle fracture. Which of the following management strategies is recommended to minimize the risk of fixation failure and Charcot arthropathy?
o: Standard ORIF and immediate weight bearing at 2 weeks
Super-construct fixation (e.g., longer plates, multiple syndesmotic screws) and prolonged non-weight bearing
Primary ankle arthrodesis with an intramedullary nail
items.e: Diabetic patients with neuropathy require "super-constructs" (more robust fixation) and often double the standard non-weight-bearing time (e.g., 12 weeks instead of 6) to prevent complications like Charcot and loss of fixation.
items.note: Tests critical management modifications for a high-risk patient group as detailed in the notes.

items.q: During the lateral approach to the fibula for an ankle fracture, which nerve is at greatest risk as it pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm proximal to the tip of the lateral malleolus and crosses the surgical field obliquely?
items.e: The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the crural fascia approximately 10-12 cm above the lateral malleolus and crosses the lateral surgical field obliquely, making it susceptible to injury during the lateral incision for fibular fixation.
items.note: Tests surgical anatomy and nerve-at-risk specific to the commonest ankle fracture approach.

items.q: Regarding the blood supply to the proximal humerus, recent studies (e.g., Hettrich et al.) have revised classical teaching. Which artery is now considered to provide the majority (approximately 64%) of the blood supply to the humeral head?
o: Ascending branch of the profunda brachii
items.e: Classically, the anterior humeral circumflex and its arcuate branch were considered the main supply, but modern studies show the posterior humeral circumflex artery provides the majority (64%) of the head's blood supply.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the shift in anatomical understanding mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: According to Hertel's criteria, which of the following radiographic features is the most reliable predictor of humeral head ischaemia following a proximal humerus fracture?
o: Metaphyseal extension of the head fragment less than 8 mm
Displacement of the surgical neck over 1 cm
items.e: Hertel's predictors of head ischaemia include metaphyseal extension attached to the head of <8 mm, a disrupted medial hinge (>2 mm displacement), and an anatomical neck fracture pattern.
items.note: The question correctly identifies one of the three key Hertel predictors specified in the notes.

items.q: An 82-year-old female sustains a displaced two-part surgical neck fracture of the humerus. She is relatively sedentary. Based on the findings of the ProFHER trial (2015), what is the most appropriate management?
o: Non-operative management with a sling and early pendulum exercises
items.e: The ProFHER trial showed no significant difference in clinical outcomes at 2 and 5 years between surgery and non-operative care for displaced proximal humerus fractures involving the surgical neck in elderly patients.
items.note: This is a high-yield clinical trial result specifically mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A 75-year-old male sustains a four-part proximal humerus fracture with significant comminution of the tuberosities. Which surgical option is currently preferred in this age group due to more predictable functional outcomes?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation with a locking plate
items.e: In elderly patients (typically >70 years) with four-part fractures, RTSA is preferred over hemiarthroplasty because functional outcomes in RTSA do not strictly depend on tuberosity healing, which is often poor in the elderly.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the current surgical preference for elderly complex fractures as per the notes.

items.q: A 22-year-old football player sustains his first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. What is the approximate risk of recurrence for this patient based on his age?
items.e: Recurrence after a first-time shoulder dislocation is strongly and inversely related to age; patients under 20 years have a recurrence risk as high as 90%.
items.note: The question tests a fundamental epidemiological fact regarding shoulder instability.

items.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a lateral third clavicle fracture. Radiographs show that the medial fragment is detached from the coracoclavicular ligaments (Neer Type II). What is the most likely clinical concern regarding this specific fracture pattern?
o: High risk of subclavian artery injury
Spontaneous healing is expected with a sling
items.e: Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures are unstable because the medial fragment is detached from the CC ligaments, leading to a high non-union rate (about 30%) if treated non-operatively.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific complication associated with Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures.

items.q: A 25-year-old patient sustains a closed midshaft humeral shaft fracture following a fall. Clinical examination reveals an inability to extend the wrist and fingers. What is the most appropriate next step in management for the nerve injury?
o: Immediate surgical exploration of the radial nerve
Observation and expectant management for 3-4 months
items.e: Radial nerve palsy in closed humeral shaft fractures is usually a neurapraxia. Spontaneous recovery occurs in 70-90% of cases, so observation for 3-4 months is the standard of care before considering EMG or exploration.
items.note: The question tests the standard conservative management protocol for this common injury.

items.q: A 30-year-old mountain biker sustains an acromioclavicular joint injury. Radiographs show a 50% increase in the coracoclavicular (CC) distance compared to the contralateral side. Which Rockwood grade is this, and what is the recommended initial management?
items.e: Rockwood Type III involves a 25-100% increase in CC distance. Current consensus recommends initial non-operative management for most Type III injuries, reserving surgery for high-demand athletes or failed conservative care.
items.note: The question correctly links the radiographic definition of Rockwood Type III with its standard initial management.

items.q: A 78-year-old woman with osteoporosis sustains a highly comminuted, intra-articular distal humerus fracture (AO/OTA 13C3). Based on the McKee trial findings for this patient group, which management strategy is likely to provide better early functional outcomes?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation with parallel plates
External fixation with early range of motion
items.e: The McKee trial demonstrated that for elderly patients with unreconstructable comminuted (C3) distal humerus fractures, total elbow arthroplasty (TEA) provides better early functional results and lower reoperation rates compared to ORIF.
items.note: The question accurately reflects the findings of a landmark trial cited in Campbell's and the provided notes regarding elderly distal humerus fractures.

items.q: When performing an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a radial shaft fracture in an adult, restoring the 'radial bow' is critical for forearm rotation. At what location along the radius (from the proximal end) is the maximal radial bow normally found?
items.e: Restoring the radial bow is essential for full forearm rotation; the maximal radial bow is located at approximately 60% of the length of the radius measured from the proximal end.
items.note: This is a classic anatomical/radiographic fact essential for forearm fracture management.

items.q: A 35-year-old male sustains a displaced, non-comminuted transverse fracture of the olecranon. The ulnohumeral joint remains stable. What is the most common complication associated with the standard surgical treatment (tension-band wiring) for this injury?
items.e: According to the Mayo classification, this is a Type IIA fracture. Tension-band wiring (TBW) is the standard treatment, but symptomatic hardware is the most common complication, with removal rates reported between 50-80%.
items.note: The complication and its frequency are well-documented in the reference notes and Campbell's.

items.q: In which of the following clinical scenarios is excision of the radial head strictly contraindicated?
o: An isolated, comminuted Mason Type III fracture with an intact interosseous membrane
A Mason Type II fracture with a mechanical block to rotation
A radial head fracture associated with an Essex-Lopresti injury
A delayed presentation of a malunited radial head fragment in a stable elbow
items.e: Radial head excision is contraindicated when there is longitudinal or transverse elbow/forearm instability, such as in Essex-Lopresti injuries (IOM disruption), MCL injuries, or coronoid fractures, as the radial head is a vital secondary stabilizer.
items.note: The contraindication is a critical 'never-event' in orthopaedic trauma to prevent proximal radial migration.

items.q: A patient presents with elbow instability following a previous lateral release for tennis elbow. On examination, a 'clunk' is felt at 40 degrees of flexion while applying a valgus load, axial load, and supination. Insufficiency of which structure is responsible for this finding?
items.e: The description defines a positive lateral pivot-shift test (O'Driscoll), which is diagnostic of posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI) caused by LUCL insufficiency.
items.note: The test and the structure involved are standard knowledge for elbow instability.

items.q: Regarding Monteggia fracture-dislocations in the adult population, which of the following statements is most accurate?
o: Bado Type I (anterior dislocation) is the most common pattern in adults
Bado Type II (posterior dislocation) is the most common pattern in adults
Non-operative management of the ulnar fracture is the treatment of choice
The radial head should be excised immediately to prevent stiffness
items.e: While Bado Type I is most common in children, Bado Type II (posterior Monteggia, often involving a radial head fracture) is the most common pattern in adults. Treatment requires anatomical ulnar plating to reduce the radial head.
items.note: The distinction between pediatric and adult Monteggia patterns is a common exam topic.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old woman falls onto an outstretched hand. X‑ray shows dorsal angulation of 25°, 4 mm radial shortening, and a 3 mm step‑off of the distal radius articular surface. According to Lafontaine’s criteria, what is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Immediate open reduction with volar locking plate
items.e: Three of Lafontaine’s predictors (dorsal angulation >20°, dorsal comminution, articular step‑off >2 mm) indicate a high risk of loss of reduction in cast. Volar locking plate fixation is recommended for such unstable fractures in young/active patients.
items.note: All data match the notes and accepted guidelines.

items.q: During a closed reduction of a distal radius fracture under haematoma block, the anesthetic is injected into:
o: Into the fracture haematoma from the dorsal side
items.e: The correct technique is intrahaematoma injection from the dorsal aspect; aspiration of blood confirms correct placement.
items.note: Matches standard procedural description.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman has an undisplaced distal radius fracture with 1.5 mm shortening and 18° radial inclination. The radiograph shows no articular step‑off. What is the most appropriate management?
items.e: The alignment is within acceptable limits; a cast for 4–6 weeks is adequate, with serial radiographs to confirm maintenance of reduction.
items.note: Consistent with treatment thresholds.

items.q: A patient with an acute distal radius fracture develops an acute carpal tunnel syndrome while in a cast. The most appropriate surgical step is:
o: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Removal of the cast and observation
Excision of the flexor retinaculum (carpal tunnel release) with provisional fixation
Removal of the cast and plan delayed fixation
items.e: Urgent carpal tunnel release is required; provisional fixation can be performed to secure the fracture while the nerve decompression is completed.
items.note: Matches the standard emergency management.

items.q:
A 27‑year‑old man presents with a Gustilo‑Anderson type IIIB tibial shaft fracture after a road traffic accident. Which statement best guides the timing of definitive soft‑tissue coverage?
A. Offer skin grafting within 12 hours to minimise infection risk
B. Delay coverage until the wound is completely clean, typically after 48 hours of debridement
C. Undertake definitive cover within 72 hours, ideally before 48 hours if an urgency score is high
D. Perform coverage only after the fracture is internally fixed and bone healing is evident
items.e: Coverage within 72 h (‘fix‑and‑flap’) is recommended for type IIIIB wounds; earlier is preferable if there is an urgency score but never delayed until after bone healing.
items.note: All statements are plausible, only C aligns with current standards.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old male sustains a closed mid‑shaft tibial fracture. The surgeon chooses an intramedullary nail for fixation. Which statement best describes the biomechanical requirement that this construct satisfies for optimal secondary bone healing?
o: Relative stability allowing micromotion within 2‑10 % strain
Absolute stability with no gap formation
Absolute stability with a thickness‑gap length ratio above 3
items.e: Intramedullary nailing provides relative stability; the allowable strain (2‑10 %) permits callus formation which is the hallmark of secondary healing.
items.note: All facts are consistent with Campbell and the question is a clear single‑best‑answer.

items.q: In a 45‑year‑old woman with a three‑part proximal humerus fracture, the surgeon applies a locking plate. The fracture is anatomically reduced but the surgeon deliberately introduces a small interfragmentary gap of 0.5 mm to promote healing. According to Perren’s strain theory, this strategy aims to maintain:
o: Strain between 2 % and 10 % for secondary healing
Strain between 0.1 % and 1 % for optimal callus
items.e: A 0.5‑mm gap with micromotion keeps strain in the 2‑10 % window, encouraging secondary healing with callus while avoiding excessive movement.
items.note: The reasoning matches Campbell’s strain limits.

items.q: A 20‑year‑old cyclist presents with a displaced distal radius fracture. The orthopaedic team repairs it with a compression plate. Which type of biological healing is most likely to occur?
o: Callus formation with intramembranous ossification only
No callus due to vascular compromise
items.e: Compression plating delivers absolute stability and interfragmentary compression; therefore, primary bone healing with no callus is expected.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell’s definition of primary healing.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old diabetic patient develops a non‑union of the distal femur four months after failed plating. Radiographs show no bridging callus but a well‑healed fracture gap with a stable construct. According to the Weber‑Cech classification, this is
items.e: The absence of callus and poor biology with a stable construct characterises an atrophic (biologically poor) non‑union.
items.note: Matches the textbook definition.

items.q: Which of the following statements best explains why a 5‑cm segmental tibial defect requires a two‑stage Masquelet technique rather than a single‑stage autograft transplant?
o: The induced membrane facilitates osteogenic cell recruitment and vascularity for large defects
A single stage risks membrane thinning and insufficient BMP release
The technique reduces donor site morbidity compared to a large autograft harvest
It avoids the need for antibiotic‑laden cement and its associated toxicity
items.e: The PMMA spacer induces a vascularised membrane rich in growth factors, which is essential for healing large (>4 cm) defects after the first stage.
items.note: Accurate description of the Masquelet sequence.

items.q: In a 25‑year‑old patient with a diaphyseal femoral fracture, the surgeon opts for an “exchange nailing” technique. What is the primary goal of this procedure?
o: Removing all scar tissue within the medullary canal
Increasing the diameter of the nail to enhance absolute stability and stimulate osteogenic response
Shortening the fragment to reduce shortening
Applying a larger plate for additional compression
items.e: Reaming larger than the previous nail and inserting a larger nail (exchange nailing) increases absolute stability, decreases strain, and provides a larger intramedullary surface for osteogenic stimulation.
items.note: Directly reflects the principle of exchange nailing.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a femoral neck fracture and a T‑score of –2.8 is started on alendronate 70 mg weekly. Two years later, she reports a persistent, throbbing pain around the left hip. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her new pain?
items.e: Intermittent hip pain in a patient on bisphosphonates can signal an atypical femoral fracture, especially after a few years of therapy.
items.note: Factually correct per Campbell and ASBMR guidance.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman on yearly zoledronate for osteoporosis develops a sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in her left eye. Ophthalmologic examination shows a shallow anterior chamber and clear cornea. What is the most likely complication?
items.e: Bisphosphonates can trigger ocular inflammation, including acute angle‑closure glaucoma, especially in predisposed individuals.
items.note: Matches known adverse effect profile.
items.reason: invented association: bisphosphonates cause uveitis/scleritis, not painless angle-closure vision loss

items.q: Which of the following dosing schedules would allow a drug holiday for a patient who has been on oral bisphosphonate therapy for five years?
o: Continue 70 mg weekly for an additional year
Switch to zoledronate 5 mg IV yearly for another year
Stop the bisphosphonate and start denosumab 60 mg monthly indefinitely
Discontinue bisphosphonate and wait 2–3 years before re‑initiating therapy
items.e: After five years of oral bisphosphonates, a 2–3‑year drug holiday is recommended if the patient is not high risk.
items.note: Aligned with ASBMR task‑force 2016.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old man with long‑term glucocorticoid therapy has a T‑score of –2.0 and a FRAX hip fracture probability of 5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.e: Patients with glucocorticoid‑induced osteoporosis and a T‑score between –1 and –2.5 with a moderate FRAX risk benefit from antiresorptive therapy, such as alendronate.
items.note: Matches guideline algorithm.

items.q: Which laboratory abnormality is most commonly associated with prolonged bisphosphonate use?
items.e: Bisphosphonates reduce bone resorption, which can precipitate hypocalcemia, especially if vitamin D is insufficient.
items.note: Standard pharmacologic effect.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old man presents with a sudden, extremely painful swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Synovial fluid shows negatively birefringent needle‑shaped crystals on compensated polarised light microscopy. Which of the following is the most important next step in management of this patient?
o: Begin oral colchicine 1.2 mg/0.6 mg dose
Order a dual‑energy CT scan of the foot
Initiate prednisolone 30 mg PO for 5 days
Send the same fluid for Gram stain and culture
items.e: The presence of crystals does not exclude septic arthritis; the gold‑standard is to send fluid for Gram stain and culture to rule out infection before starting anti‑inflammatory therapy.
items.note: Standard practice per Campbell’s: send fluid for both crystal analysis and microbiology.

items.q: During an acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease stage 3, which antirheumatic drug should be avoided due to a high risk of nephrotoxicity and gastrointestinal complications?
o: Oral NSAIDs at full anti‑inflammatory dose
items.e: Full‑dose NSAIDs are contraindicated in CKD 3 as they worsen renal function and increase GI bleeding risk; colchicine, steroids and anakinra are safer alternatives.
items.note: Guidelines and Campbell’s classify NSAIDs as high‑risk in CKD ≥ 3.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old woman with a history of hypertension and metabolic syndrome attends with a sudden onset of knee pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis reveals a high WBC count of 35,000/mm³ and weakly positive birefringent rhomboid crystals. Which disorder is implicated in the formation of these crystals?
items.e: Weakly positive birefringent rhomboid (or rod‑shaped) crystals are classic for calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD, pseudogout).
items.note: Crystal morphology is diagnostic.

items.q: The double‑contour sign seen on ultrasound of a joint is most characteristic for which crystal arthropathy?
items.e: The double‑contour sign represents monosodium urate coating the cartilage surface, a hallmark imaging feature of gout.
items.note: Ultrasound evidence from Campbell’s.

items.q: A patient with longstanding uncontrolled hyperuricaemia presents with an irradiating pain over the lateral elbow and a markedly swollen, tender olecranon bursa. Radiograph shows a punched‑out erosion with overhanging edges and a soft‑tissue mass that is chalky white on palpation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Chalky white tophi with characteristic erosions are typical of tophaceous gout.
items.note: Radiographic description matches gout erosions.

items.q: A 48‑year‑old man on diuretic therapy develops severe flank pain and bilateral pink urine. Renal ultrasound shows echogenic foci in the cortical parenchyma. Which metabolic derangement is most likely responsible for these findings?
items.e: Diuretics can precipitate hyperoxaluria; calcium oxalate crystals deposit in the renal cortex, producing echogenic foci.
items.note: Clinical context of diuretics and imaging matches oxalate deposition.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old male presents with a painless, progressive enlargement of the left femur and low‑grade fever. Plain X‑ray shows an osteolytic flare followed by cortical thickening and bone enlargement. Which of these investigations is most useful to determine disease activity?
items.e: Serum alkaline phosphatase rises with active bone remodelling in Paget’s disease and is the best marker of disease activity.
items.note: Straightforward, standard fact

items.q: Which site is least commonly affected by Paget disease of bone?
items.e: Hands and feet are rarely involved; pelvis, skull and lumbar spine are typical sites.
items.note: Clear anatomical knowledge

items.q: A biopsy of a lytic skull lesion in an elderly patient shows woven bone with a jigsaw arrangement of reversal lines and giant, multinucleated osteoclasts. What genetic mutation is most likely implicated?
items.e: SQSTM1 (p62) mutations are found in about 40% of familial Paget’s disease and 5–10% of sporadic cases.
items.note: Genetic association

items.q: In a patient with polyostotic Paget disease, which of these clinical features is most characteristic of the disease’s systemic metabolic effect?
items.e: High‑output cardiac failure occurs in extensive disease due to increased vascular shunting.
items.note: Systemic sequelae

items.q: Which of the following is the preferred initial bisphosphonate therapy for active Paget disease?
items.e: IV zoledronic acid 5 mg once is most effective and achieves rapid ALP normalization.
items.note: Treatment guidelines

items.q: A 38‑year‑old man receiving high‑dose oral prednisolone for a renal allograft presents with right groin pain that exacerbates with weight‑bearing. Plain AP pelvis shows no abnormality, but MRI of the hip shows a serpiginous low‑signal band on T1 and a double‑line sign on T2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Aseptic necrosis of the femoral head
items.e: The imaging described is classic for osteonecrosis (AVN) – the T1 low‑signal band and T2 double‑line sign are pathognomonic.
items.note: Correctness verified against standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: In a patient with steroid‑associated ONFH, which of the following is the best screening test to detect early disease before radiographic changes?
items.e: MRI is 99 % sensitive for early, pre‑radiographic osteonecrosis and is the gold standard for screening the contralateral hip.
items.note: Standard imaging pathway confirmed.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old smoker male presents with sudden worsening of morning hip pain. Radiographs show a radiolucent subchondral line on frog‑leg lateral view but no other changes. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.e: The crescent sign indicates a subchondral fracture; MRI is needed to assess extent and plan early intervention such as core decompression.
items.note: Recognition of the 'crescent sign' as a fracture precursor.

items.q: Which of the following best explains why the femoral head in adults is so vulnerable to ischemia following a displaced femoral neck fracture?
o: Loss of the medial femoral circumflex artery territory
Loss of the lateral femoral circumflex artery territory
Injury to the artery of the ligamentum teres
Fracture of the ossification centre of the femoral head
items.e: The medial femoral circumflex artery, via its posterosuperior retinacular branches, supplies most of the adult femoral head; its disruption leads to AVN.
items.note: Anatomical supply consistent with Campbell's.

items.q: A 30‑year‑old patient with sickle cell disease presents with left hip pain. MRI shows the double‑line sign. Which surgical approach preserves the main blood supply to the femoral head?
o: Posterior approach with short external rotator repair
items.e: Ganz surgical dislocation allows safe access while preserving the medial femoral circumflex artery’s retinacular branches.
items.note: Surgical anatomy guideline.
items.reason: flawed premise: no standard approach-choice question for sickle ONFH; options not comparable

items.q: In the architecture of cortical bone, the ‘hole zones’ in collagen fibrils are:
items.e: Mineral nucleates in the gaps (“hole zones”) between collagen molecules during matrix mineralisation.
items.note: Standard bone biology concept

items.q: Which of the following proteins, produced by osteoblasts and requiring vitamin K‑dependent γ‑carboxylation, serves as the most abundant non‑collagenous bone matrix protein and a serum marker of bone formation?
items.e: Osteocalcin is the major non‑collagenous protein, γ‑carboxylated by vitamin K, and its serum level reflects bone formation activity.
items.note: Unambiguous correct answer

items.q: The RANKL–RANK interaction is essential for osteoclastogenesis. Which cell type is the principal source of RANKL that stimulates osteoclast precursors in normal bone?
items.e: Osteoblasts and osteocytes produce RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive differentiation and activation.
items.note: Clear, field‑standard answer

items.q: During bone mineralisation, which of the following processes contributes directly to the removal of the mineralisation inhibitor pyrophosphate?
items.e: Alkaline phosphatase hydrolyses extracellular pyrophosphate, reducing its inhibitory effect and allowing hydroxyapatite crystal growth.
items.note: Standard pathophysiology

items.q: Which of the following best describes the composition of the superficial zone (lamina splendens) of articular cartilage?
items.e: The superficial zone has the highest water & collagen content and the lowest proteoglycan, giving it a smooth, lubricated surface.
items.note: Answer C is factually correct.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with an isolated loose body in her wrist joint. Synovial biopsy shows cartilaginous nodules attached to the synovium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Primary synovial chondromatosis originates from metaplastic synovial cells that produce cartilaginous nodules, forming loose bodies.
items.note: Correct answer B matches classic pathology.

items.q: Which type of collagen is predominantly found in fibrocartilage such as the meniscus and annulus fibrosus?
items.e: Fibrocartilage is rich in type I collagen, which provides tensile strength to these structures.
items.note: Answer A is correct.

items.q: The ratio of chondroitin‑4 to keratan sulfate in articular cartilage:
o: Decreases with age but rises in osteoarthritis
Is highest in the superficial zone
items.e: Chondroitin‑4 sulfate falls with age, while keratan sulfate increases, so the ratio decreases; in OA the ratio rises again due to matrix changes.
items.note: Answer C is accurate.

items.q: Which matrix protein acts as a boundary lubricant secreted by superficial zone chondrocytes and synovial cells?
items.e: Lubricin (PRG4) is the principal boundary lubricant, preventing wear between articular surfaces.
items.note: Correct answer B.

items.q: A surgeon plans to cement a femoral intertrochanteric fracture with acrylic bone cement. Considering the mechanical properties listed, which material will most closely match the elastic modulus of cortical bone, thereby reducing stress shielding around the fixation site?
items.e: Cortical bone has an elastic modulus of about 15–20 GPa, while titanium alloys are close to 110 GPa—much nearer to bone than the much stiffer ceramic, CoCr, or the very compliant PMMA.
items.note: All facts match the reference table.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old man presents with a spiral fracture of the tibial shaft 7 days after a motorcycle crash. In the absence of implant removal, which type of bone defect would most severely compromise the remaining torsional strength of the healed tibia?
o: A small cortical screw hole (~15% of diameter)
An open longitudinal slot removing ~25% of the cortical circumference
A percutaneous drilling for a nail entry point (~2 mm diameter)
A unicortical osteotomy at the distal tibial metaphysis
items.e: Open‑section (slot) defects remove a large perimeter of healthy cortical bone, drastically reducing torsional strength—often over 50%—more than a round cavity of equivalent size.
items.note: Consistent with defect‑strength relationships in the notes.

items.q: During a routine postoperative check, a patient’s X‑ray shows a small radiolucent line around a titanium plate. The surgeon recalls that titanium is notch‑sensitive. Which of the following actions should be taken to prevent a fatigue fracture?
o: Polish the plate surface to reduce scratches
Apply a thicker titanium sleeve over the plate
Bend the plate back and forth to condition it
Replace the plate with a cobalt‑chromium one
items.e: Polishing removes surface scratches that act as stress risers; titanium is prone to notching, so smoothing the surface reduces the likelihood of fatigue failure.
items.note: Matches the guideline in the notes.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old athlete suffers an anterior cruciate ligament tear. Under rapid loading, the ligament is most likely to fail how?
items.e: Fast loading causes ligament failure mid‑substance; slower loading tends to result in avulsion at the insertion.
items.note: Matches viscoelastic loading comments.

items.q: A research team is testing a novel bioceramic implant. On a stress‑strain curve, the material shows a high Young’s modulus but a low ultimate tensile strength. What clinical concern does this raise?
o: It will be too brittle for load‑bearing use
It will be too ductile and prone to plastic deformation
Its hardness will cause wear against bone
It will have poor fatigue resistance
items.e: High modulus with low ultimate strength indicates brittleness—failure may occur under a sudden load before showing plastic deformation.
items.note: Consistent with definition of brittleness.

items.q: In a closed femoral shaft fracture treated with a locking compression plate, which of the following is NOT a necessary condition for secondary (callus) bone healing?
o: Absolute stability with compression across the fracture gap
items.e: Secondary healing requires relative stability (micromotion) and interfragmentary strain 2‑10 %; absolute compression would favour primary healing.
items.note: Matches strain theory.

items.q: During a sural nerve graft harvest, sensory loss is usually most pronounced over which area of the foot?
items.e: The sural nerve supplies the lateral aspect of the foot; therefore, harvesting it causes sensory loss in that region.
items.note: Correct and unambiguous.

items.q: In a randomized controlled trial comparing two surgical techniques, the investigators use a central telephone system to allocate participants. Which bias is this method specifically aimed to prevent?
items.e: Allocation concealment via a central system prevents selection bias by ensuring the enrolling clinician cannot predict the next assignment.
items.note: Central allocation prevents selection bias.

items.q: Which statement best describes the primary advantage of an intention‑to‑treat analysis in a superiority trial?
o: It accounts for cross‑overs by analyzing only those who completed treatment
It preserves the benefits of randomisation
It allows for per‑protocol withdrawals to be excluded
items.e: ITT analyses maintain the initial random allocation, preventing bias introduced by post‑randomisation events.
items.note: ITT preserves randomisation.

items.q: A systematic review includes five RCTs; all report similar outcomes with narrow confidence intervals. According to GRADE, what would the quality of evidence likely be?
items.e: A consistent body of well‑conducted RCTs yields high‑quality evidence unless downgraded for risk of bias or imprecision.
items.note: Consistent, precise RCTs = high GRADE.

items.q: Which bias is most likely when patients who develop a complication are more likely to be lost to follow‑up than those who remain well?
items.e: Differential loss to follow‑up that depends on outcome creates attrition bias.
items.note: Outcome‑dependent loss → attrition bias.

items.q: In a retrospective cohort study, missing data on smoking status were imputed using multiple imputation. Which type of confounding is this technique attempting to address?
items.e: Imputing missing values on a known confounder (smoking) helps control for measured confounding.
items.note: Imputation handles missing measured confounders.
items.reason: flawed premise: multiple imputation addresses missing data, not a type of confounding

items.q: A trial comparing a new bone graft substitute with autograft reports a 10 % non‑union rate in the experimental group and 12 % in the control. The study’s authors declare non‑inferiority with a margin of 5 %. Which statement is correct regarding the interpretation of the results?
o: The experimental graft is superior to autograft
The experimental graft is non‑inferior to autograft
The experimental graft is inferior to autograft
The margin was too large to draw any conclusion
items.e: Because the 95 % CI for the difference lies within the 5 % margin, non‑inferiority is demonstrated.
items.note: 2% ≤ 5% margin → non‑inferior.

items.q: Which characteristic of a diagnostic study places it at level I evidence for diagnostic accuracy?
o: Testing the diagnostic tool in a non‑consecutive sample against an imperfect reference standard
Testing previously validated criteria in consecutive patients against a universal reference standard
Using a case‑control design with a known disease prevalence
Retrospective chart review of patients who underwent the test
items.e: Level I diagnostic studies test the criteria on consecutive patients using a perfect reference standard.
items.note: Consecutive + perfect reference = level I.

items.q: A junior orthopaedic resident is setting up a fluoroscopic procedure for a right ankle arthroscopy. He asks which orientation of the C‑arm cable would give the lowest dose to the surgeon’s hands. Which is the best choice?
o: Tube under the table, image intensifier above the patient
Tube above the table, image intensifier below the patient
Tube and intensifier both above the table
Tube and intensifier both below the table
items.e: Placement of the tube under the patient and the image intensifier above it keeps the anterior scanner closest to the patient and the beam entrance side farthest from the surgeon, thereby minimizing scatter and hand dose.
items.note: Orientation matches radiation‑physics principles cited in the notes.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old man receives a radiograph of his right knee. The AP film shows a faint white line on the medial tibial plateau. Which physical phenomenon is most responsible for this increased radiodensity?
items.e: The photoelectric effect, whose probability rises with Z³/E³, dominates at low photon energies in high‑Z materials such as bone, giving the white appearance of the tibial plateau.
items.note: Photoelectric predominance in cortical bone is standard radiology knowledge.

items.q: During a routine chest radiograph, a nurse incorrectly uses an aluminium filter of 5 mm thickness. How does this alter the patient’s absorbed skin dose compared to no filter?
o: Has no effect on absorbed dose
Increases scattered radiation but not absorbed dose
items.e: Aluminium filtration removes low‑energy photons that would otherwise be absorbed by the skin; thus the filter reduces the absorbed (skin) dose by roughly 20 % while slightly increasing the average beam energy.
items.note: Filtration effect on skin dose is a well‑documented fact.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon wants to estimate the whole‑body stochastic risk after a lumbar spine CT scan. Which unit best represents that risk?
items.e: The stochastic risk is expressed in Sieverts, which account for absorbed dose weighted by tissue sensitivity; Gray measures only absorbed energy.
items.note: Direct mapping of radiation terminology.

items.q: A staff member standing 1.5 m from the patient during fluoroscopy reports a sharp increase in scatter dose when the C‑arm is rotated 45° left‑to‑right. What explains this change?
o: Inverse square law reduces scatter at larger angles
Collimation is less effective when the beam is off‑axis
Scatter originates mostly from the tube side and increases with beam path length
The image intensifier’s design limits scatter reduction at oblique angles
items.e: Scatter rises with the length of patient tissue the beam traverses; rotating the arm off‑axis increases that path length, so scatter dose rises even though the distance is unchanged.
items.note: Radiation physics of scatter with beam path length.

items.q: In a CT head scan, the effective dose is reported as 2 mSv. Compared with the annual natural background dose of 2.4 mSv, this scan is equivalent to how many months of background exposure?
items.e: 2 mSv ÷ 2.4 mSv yr⁻¹ ≈ 0.83 yr, which is about 10 months. The nearest option to 10 months is 9 months, so the corrected answer should be (D) 9 months. This aligns with the notes’ style of rounding to the nearest given choice.
items.note: Mathematical correction of the answer.
items.reason: key and explanation contradictory; arithmetic error

items.q: A 30‑year‑old male is brought to the ED after a fall from height. Physical exam shows a widened symphysis pubis on pelvis AP X‑ray but AP distance <2.5 cm. There is no vertical displacement of the hemipelvis. According to the Young‑Burgess classification, this is:
items.e: APC I involves symphysis widening <2.5 cm with intact SI ligaments – a rotationally stable, non‑operative injury.
items.note: Result matches standard Young‑Burgess criteria.

items.q: A 78‑year‑old woman falls at home and presents with groin pain. Plain AP pelvis and lateral hip radiographs show a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture with posterior tilt of 22°. Which surgical option is most appropriate?
o: Arthroscopic reduction and fixation with cannulated screws
Cemented hemiarthroplasty via the anterolateral approach
items.e: The posterior tilt >20° predicts early failure of intracapsular fixation in elderly frail patients. Cemented hemiarthroplasty provides immediate weight‑bearing and reduces periprosthetic fracture risk.
items.note: Posterior tilt threshold validated by literature.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old male sustains a Pauwels type III femoral neck fracture (≥50°) after a motor vehicle accident. What is the preferred fixation technique to counter the vertical shear forces?
o: Large‑diameter lag screw with an anti‑rotation screw
Dynamic hip screw with a supplementary anti‑rotation screw
items.e: A fixed‑angle cephalomedullary nail spreads the shear load and provides a stable construct for vertical Pauwels III fractures, whereas sliding devices would fail under shear.
items.note: Fixed‑angle construct recommended for high Pauwels angle.
items.reason: wrong key and repeats an existing question

items.q: During the initial evaluation of a patient with a suspected intertrochanteric fracture, which radiographic measurement is critical for predicting screw cut‑out with a DHS?
items.e: Tip‑apex distance (≤25 mm) is the operative predictor of cut‑out; lengths longer than 25 mm markedly increase failure risk.
items.note: TAD threshold is well established.

items.q: An elderly patient with an AO/OTA 31A2.3 intertrochanteric fracture has a lateral wall thickness of 18 mm. Which implant choice is most justified?
o: Sliding hip screw with a large side plate
Plate and screws in a Judet configuration
items.e: A lateral wall <20.5 mm signifies instability; a cephalomedullary nail is indicated to avoid cut‑out and provide better stability.
items.note: Lateral wall rule for implant selection.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old runner develops prodromal thigh pain after 3 years on bisphosphonate therapy. Radiographs reveal a transverse fracture line with a medial spike in the subtrochanteric region. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: External fixation with a split‑ring frame
items.e: The bony picture meets ASBMR criteria for an atypical femoral fracture; prophylactic intramedullary nailing prevents complete fracture and is the standard of care.
items.note: Standard AFF management protocol.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old woman falls from a bed onto her left knee. Radiographs show a medial plateau fracture with 5 mm widening and no displacement. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Percutaneous drilling followed by bone grafting
items.e: Non‑operative care is acceptable for low‑energy, minimally displaced fractures that are stable in extension, especially in low‑function elderly patients.
items.note: Guideline for non‑operative treatment.
items.reason: contradictory premise (widening without displacement); medial plateau fractures are usually operative

items.q: Which imaging study is mandatory before definitive fixation of any operatively managed tibial plateau fracture?
o: CT scan of the distal tibia
Ultrasound of the medial collateral ligament
items.e: CT provides precise 3‑dimensional anatomy of the articular surface, guiding reduction and fixation; it becomes routine for all operative tibial plateau fractures.
items.note: Routine practice in operative plateau fractures.

items.q: A 36‑year‑old man with a type VI tibial plateau fracture undergoes a spanning external fixator the day after injury. Why is a staged approach preferred?
o: Soft‑tissue edema resolves earlier than bone healing
It reduces the need for multiple surgeries
It eliminates the risk of compartment syndrome
items.e: High‑energy fractures with soft‑tissue compromise require a staged plan; the external fixator restores length and alignment while the soft tissues recover before definitive ORIF.
items.note: Standard high‑energy fracture protocol.

items.q: During a posteromedial approach to a tibial plateau fracture, the interval between which structures is used to protect the popliteal neurovascular bundle?
o: Gastrocnemius medial head and pes anserinus or semimembranosus
Tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus
items.e: The posteromedial interval lies between the medial head of gastrocnemius (retracted) and the pes anserinus/semimembranosus, providing safe access while preserving the neurovascular structures.
items.note: Anatomical landmark in posteromedial approach.

items.q: A type IV medial tibial plateau fracture is associated with which complication that mandates urgent vascular assessment?
items.e: Type IV fractures are high‑energy and fracture‑dislocation injuries; the popliteal artery runs in the posterior compartment and is at risk, necessitating prompt evaluation.
items.note: Classical teaching of vascular injury in medial plateau fractures.

items.q: On a mortise view of an ankle fracture, the tibial plafond appears to have a 25% articular fragment posteriorly. Which posterior malleolar classification does this fragment best fit?
items.e: Posterior malleolar fragments that are posterolateral and oblique fall into Haraguchi type I, the most common posterior malleolar pattern.
items.note: All information aligns with Campbell’s classification.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old man with a Weber C fibular fracture is found to have a widened tibiofibular clear space on the AP view. What is the most appropriate next step regarding the syndesmotic injury?
o: Manually reduce the ankle and leave it in a cast for 4 weeks
Apply a syndesmotic screw immediately with a 4‑mm lag
Observe and perform stress radiographs after 2 weeks
items.e: A widened tibiofibular clear space indicates a syndesmotic injury; an immediate syndesmotic screw fixation (4 mm) stabilises the syndesmosis.
items.note: Standard practice per Campbell and the Ottawa rules.

items.q: During surgical fixation of a bimalleolar ankle fracture, the surgeon decides to use a posterolateral antiglide plate for the fibula. The main advantage of this plate over a traditional one‑third tubular plate in a Weber B fracture is:
o: Reduced risk of postoperative peroneal nerve injury
Greater biomechanical strength with less hardware prominence
items.e: The posterolateral antiglide plate provides superior biomechanical stability, is less prominent under the skin, and reduces soft‑tissue irritation compared with the standard one‑third tubular plate.
items.note: Matches Campbell’s recommendation.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old male suffers a closed ankle fracture with a 30% posterior malleolar fragment and intact anterior syndesmotic ligaments on MRI. Which of the following indications supports operative fixation of the posterior fragment?
o: Fragment exceeds 25% of the articular surface
items.e: Any of the listed criteria—>25% articular surface involvement, posterior talar subluxation, or an impacted fragment—warrant operative fixation of the posterior malleolus.
items.note: Directly from Campbell’s operative orthopaedics.

items.q: A 42‑year‑old woman sustained a distal fibula fracture with a lateral malleolar rupture of the deltoid ligament as seen on lateral radiograph. The medial clear space is 4 mm on the AP view but normal on a weight‑bearing mortise. What is the preferred management?
o: Immediate ORIF of the fibula and open repair of the deltoid
Closed reduction and cast immobilisation with delayed weight bearing
Closed reduction, fixation of the fibula, and weight‑bearing as tolerated
Closed reduction, fixation of the fibula, and delayed deltoid repair
items.e: Because the medial clear space normalizes on weight‑bearing, the injury is stable; ORIF of the fibula alone with early weight bearing is adequate.
items.note: Consistent with the Ottawa rules and Campbell’s indications for deltoid repair.

items.q: A 67‑year‐old woman presents with a displaced two‑part surgical neck fracture of the humerus. Radiographs show a metaphyseal extension of the fracture <8 mm and an undisturbed medial calcar. According to Hertel’s criteria, what is the most likely risk for avascular necrosis?
items.e: Hertel’s predictors indicate a low risk of AVN when the metaphyseal extension <8 mm, medial hinge intact, and no anatomical neck fracture. Thus the risk is very low (≈5 %).
items.note: firm evidence from Hertel study

items.q: A 70‑year‑old patient with a comminuted four‑part proximal humerus fracture and a 40 % head split is treated with reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Which outcome factor is least dependent on tuberosity healing?
items.e:
Reverse TSA gains most of its function from the deltoid, so internal rotation (cuff dependent) is least affected by tuberosity healing.
(D – abduction is also deltoid‑driven, but external rotation is cuff‑dependent.)
items.note: pathomechanics of reverse TSA

items.q: A 45‑year‑old presents after a fall with a displaced transverse fracture of the olecranon (Mayo Class II, non‑comminuted).  The most appropriate fixation technique is:
o: Excision of the fragment and triceps advancement
items.e: With a transverse, non‑comminuted olecranon fracture, tension‑band wiring converts triceps tension into compressive forces across the articular surface and is the standard fixation.
items.note: Standard fixation technique

items.q: In a Mason I radial head fracture with no displacement and no mechanical block, the recommended post‑injury management is:
o: Early mobilisation after aspiration of haemarthrosis
Immobilise in a cast for 4 weeks
items.e: Mason I fractures are treated non‑operatively; early mobilisation after haemarthrosis aspiration both improves function and checks for mechanical block.
items.note: Conservative treatment

items.q: Which clinical test demonstrates posterolateral rotatory instability of the elbow?
items.e: The lateral pivot‑shift test produces a clunk during flexion‑supination‑valgus loading that is characteristic of LUCL insufficiency in PLRI.
items.note: Specific PLRI test

items.q: When placing headless compression screws in a radial head fracture, the ‘safe zone’ that avoids impingement on the proximal radioulnar joint is located:
o: Directly anterior to the radial head
Laterally between the radial styloid and Lister's tubercle
items.e: In neutral rotation the non‑articular arc—between the radial styloid and Lister's tubercle—provides a ~90° window where screws can be buried without contacting the DRUJ.
items.note: Anatomical safe zone

items.q: A 75‑year‑old man with an eccentric, displaced olecranon fracture and low functional demands is best managed by:
o: Early motion with a posterior splint
items.e: In elderly low‑demand patients, a displaced olecranon fracture can often be treated non‑operatively; early mobilisation gives satisfactory function without the morbidity of hardware.
items.note: Elderly low‑demand management

items.q: According to Lafontaine’s instability predictors, which combination would most strongly suggest that a cast will fail to maintain a distal radius fracture reduction?
o: Dorsal angulation >20°, dorsal comminution, intra‑articular involvement
Ulnar variance >3 mm, age 55, no comminution
Radial inclination <15°, no ulnar fracture, age 60
items.e: The classic predictors are dorsal angulation >20°, dorsal comminution, and intra‑articular involvement; having all three signals high instability.
items.note: Matches Campbell’s instability criteria

items.q: When placing a volar locking plate for a Colles’ fracture, the plate should be positioned in relation to the watershed line to minimise risk of flexor pollicis longus rupture. The recommended location is:
o: Proximal 1 cm beyond the watershed line
Distal 1 cm proximal to the watershed line
Distal 5 mm beyond the watershed line
items.e: Keeping the plate 1 cm proximal to the watershed line reduces prominence and protects the FPL tendon.
items.note: Standard surgical practice stated in references

items.q: The DRAFFT trial compared which two fixation methods for dorsally displaced distal radius fractures?
o: Volar locking plate vs external fixation
K‑wire fixation vs volar locking plate
items.e: It showed no difference in outcome at 12 months between K‑wire fixation and volar plating.
items.note: Trial design matches literature

items.q: For a displaced waist fracture of the scaphoid, the most stable percutaneous screw trajectory is:
o: Along the central axis of the bone
items.e: A central, long screw provides the greatest compressive stability across the scaphoid waist.
items.note: Consensus in operative orthopaedics texts

items.q: Displacement of a scaphoid fracture is considered significant when:
items.e: The threshold for considering fixation is a displacement of more than 1 mm.
items.note: Standard definition in Campbell

items.q: Which of the following is an acceptable postoperative radial inclination after reduction of a distal radius fracture?
items.e: The normal inclination is 22–23°, but after reduction a maintained inclination over about 15° is acceptable.
items.note: Campbell’s retail acceptable range

items.q: A 30‑year‑old male sustains a midshaft tibial fracture that is fixed with a standard intramedullary nail. Postoperatively, he develops a patchy, firm swelling over the distal third of the tibia after two months. Which mechanism best explains the absence of callus at the fracture site?
o: Inadequate vascular supply due to periosteal stripping
Poor biological environment from systemic smoking
items.e: The nailing provided relative stability, but the strain (>10%) exceeded the range for secondary bone healing (2‑10%), leading to a fibrous union – a classic sign of poor biological response to high strain.
items.note: Clear single answer; stems match answer; options are plausible distractors.

items.q: In a 50‑year‑old diabetic patient with a distal femur shaft fracture fixed by a locked compression plate, the surgeon wants to augment biology. Which graft choice offers all three bone‑engineering properties (osteogenic, osteoconductive, osteoinductive)?
items.e: Only autologous iliac crest cancellous graft contains live cells (osteogenic), a scaffold (osteoconductive) and BMPs (osteoinductive).
items.note: Directly matches Campbell’s description.

items.q: A patient presents with a 6‑cm segmental defect of the tibial diaphysis after an open fracture. Which staged procedure is most appropriate to achieve biological bone reconstruction while preserving the vascular supply?
o: Immediate reconstruction with a vascularised fibula flap
Ilizarov bone transport with a ground plate
Masquelet induced‑membrane technique with PMMA spacer
Intramedullary reaming and grafting with cancellous autograft
items.e: The Masquelet technique involves a PMMA spacer that induces a vascular membrane, then later insertion of autograft, ideal for a 6‑cm defect with preserved vascularity.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell’s staged approach for >5‑cm defects.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a history of a low‑energy wrist fracture and a femoral neck T‑score of –2.8 is started on oral alendronate 70 mg weekly. Three months later she experiences a burst‑type atypical femoral fracture while walking on a tight‑rope. Which statement about this complication is most accurate?
o: It is most common in patients who have received zoledronate monthly for cancer
It usually occurs in the subtrochanteric region after at least 5 years of bisphosphonate therapy
It can be prevented by prescribing calcium and vitamin D alone
It is unrelated to the duration of bisphosphonate treatment
items.e: Atypical femoral fractures are rare complications of long‑term bisphosphonates and typically occur after 5‑8 years of therapy, most commonly in the subtrochanteric or femoral shaft region.
items.note: Statement B is the only accurate description.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with chronic kidney disease on a thiazide diuretic presents with a swelling knee. Synovial fluid shows rhomboid, weakly positive birefringent crystals. Which radiographic finding best characterises the late disease stage of this crystal arthropathy?
o: Subchondral cysts and joint space narrowing
Scalloping of subchondral bone with overhanging edges
Joint space preservation with punched‑out erosions and sclerotic margins
items.e: CPPD produces a classic ‘scalloped’ appearance of the subchondral bone with overhanging edges as the disease progresses. The other choices describe changes typical of osteoarthritis (A), gout (C, though erosions are also seen in gout but without scalloping), or rheumatoid arthritis (D).
items.note: Answer B correctly identifies the CPPD hallmark.

items.q: During an urgent arthrocentesis for suspected septic arthritis, needle‑shaped crystals are observed under compensated polarised light. Which additional test should always accompany the crystal analysis to avoid missed diagnosis?
o: Gram stain and culture of the aspirate
items.e: The presence of crystals does not rule out infection; therefore, a Gram stain and culture of the joint fluid must always be performed.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell’s and standard orthopaedic practice.

items.q: A patient with diabetes and hypertension presents with acute monoarthritis of the wrist. Synovial fluid shows negatively birefringent needle crystals. Which metabolic disorder is most likely contributing to the crystal deposition?
items.e: Diuretics, especially thiazides, impair urate excretion and are a common cause of hyperuricaemia leading to gout.
items.note: Alignment with pathophysiology.

items.q: Which of the following crystal types is NOT birefringent under polarised light?
items.e: Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) deposits are not birefringent; they are visualised by alizarin‑red staining or electron microscopy.
items.note: Fact stated in notes.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old man presents with dull aching back pain and a markedly raised serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 850 IU/L while his serum calcium and phosphate remain normal. Plain radiographs show an enlarged, “picture‑frame” lumbar vertebra. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Radiographic picture‑frame vertebra and elevated ALP with normal calcium classic for Paget disease; prostate metastases are osteoblastic but usually preserve normal ALP.
items.note: All facts match Campbell’s; single best answer exists.

items.q: During a routine bone scan for a suspected polyostotic metabolic bone disorder, a 55‑year‑old woman shows intense, diffuse uptake in the pelvis, proximal femora, and ribs. Which laboratory test would best confirm that the bone scan reflects Paget disease rather than a benign skeletal condition?
items.e: Paget disease is characterised by a markedly raised bone‑specific ALP reflecting increased bone turnover; calcium, vitamin‑D and PTH are usually normal.
items.note: Clear, single‑answer question.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old patient with longstanding polyostotic Paget disease develops sudden, severe right knee pain. X‑ray shows a transverse “banana” fracture of the subtrochanteric femur. Which statement about this fracture is TRUE?
o: It is usually a complete fracture that heals in 4–6 weeks
It is most often a stress fracture that occurs in the concave side of the bowed femur
It has a high rate of delayed union or non‑union
It occurs only in monostotic Paget disease
items.e: Subtrochanteric “banana” fractures in Paget are transverse, frequently occur on the concave side, and have a high incidence of delayed union or non‑union.
items.note: Consistent with Campbell; distractors are clearly wrong.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of Paget disease in a population study?
items.e: Paget disease is uncommon in Asia; it is more common in the UK, western Europe, and their emigrants. Male predominance, age rise, and rarity before 40 are well established.
items.note: Unambiguous single best answer.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old man on long‑term bisphosphonate therapy for Paget disease develops a fever and a rapidly enlarging left proximal femoral mass. Radiographs reveal lytic bone destruction with a soft‑tissue component. What is the most probable diagnosis?
items.e: New, painful, progressive lesions with soft‑tissue mass in Paget bone most suggestive of Paget sarcoma, the most common osteosarcoma in patients >60.
items.note: Standard teaching from Campbell.

items.q: In the management of Paget disease, which of the following investigations is considered the gold standard for mapping disease extent at initial diagnosis?
items.e: A whole‑body isotope bone scan shows intense uptake in all affected bones and is recommended to delineate polyostotic disease on initial presentation.
items.note: Single clear answer.

items.q: A 38‑year‑old male presents with insidious groin pain that worsens with weight bearing. Plain AP pelvis is normal. Which imaging modality is the most sensitive for early detection of osteonecrosis of the femoral head in this patient?
items.e: MRI is about 99 % sensitive and specific for early, pre‑radiographic osteonecrosis, making it the investigation of choice.
items.note: All facts match Campbell and the stem is fair.

items.q: On MRI of a subchondral lesion in the femoral head, a ‘double‑line sign’ is seen. Which line is the inner, high‑signal component?
items.e: The inner bright line represents hyperaemic granulation tissue; the outer low‑signal line is sclerotic bone, together forming the pathognomonic double‑line sign.
items.note: Correct anatomical description; distractor confuses the two lines.
items.reason: answer repeats the stem; not exam-worthy

items.q: Which lesion on plain radiograph best predicts imminent subchondral collapse in osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: The crescent sign is a subchondral radiolucent line indicating fracture and is a harbinger of collapse.
items.note: Classic orthopaedic teaching.

items.q: Which of the following statements about the vascular supply to the adult femoral head is FALSE?
o: The medial femoral circumflex artery supplies the majority of the head
The artery of the ligamentum teres provides a substantial contribution to the fovea
The deep branch of the MFCA passes posterior to obturator externus
The lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the inferior metaphyseal region
items.e: The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes only a minor share; it is not a substantial source of blood to the femoral head.
items.note: Statement B is the incorrect one.

items.q: In a patient with a deficiency of vitamin K, which bone matrix protein will be most affected, leading to impaired mineralization?
items.e: Osteocalcin requires vitamin K‑dependent gamma‑carboxylation; without it the protein cannot bind calcium, impairing mineral deposition.
items.note: Correct terminology and physiology

items.q: A child presents with generalized bone fragility and renal tubular acidosis. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the TCIRG1 gene. Which of the following best explains the clinical picture?
o: Loss of osteoblast alkaline phosphatase activity
items.e: TCIRG1 encodes a subunit of the H⁺‑ATPase; mutation abolishes acidification of the resorption compartment, causing osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis.
items.note: Clear genotype‑phenotype correlation

items.q: Which change in the RANKL:OPG ratio most directly promotes osteoclast activation during estrogen deficiency?
items.e: Estrogen loss raises RANKL and lowers OPG, tipping the ratio toward osteoclastogenesis.
items.note: Consistent with endocrine regulation of bone

items.q: The γ‑carboxylation of a specific lysine residue in osteocalcin requires which cofactor?
items.e: γ‑Carboxylation is a vitamin K‑dependent post‑translational modification of osteocalcin, enabling calcium binding. Vitamin K, not vitamin C or iron, is essential here.
items.note: Corrected factual error and clarified protein

items.q: Osteocytes sense mechanical loading primarily through which of the following mechanisms?
o: Fluid shear stress in the lacuno‑canaliculi
items.e: Osteocytes detect fluid movement around their dendrites; this mechanotransduction regulates bone remodeling.
items.note: Accurate mechanobiology

items.q: Alkaline phosphatase released by osteoblasts contributes to mineralization by:
items.e: ALP removes the mineralisation inhibitor pyrophosphate, allowing calcium and phosphate to precipitate in the matrix.
items.note: Well‑known enzymology

items.q: Loss of function of the sclerostin protein leads to which of the following skeletal phenotypes?
items.e: Sclerostin is an osteocyte‑derived Wnt antagonist; its absence causes sclerosteosis, marked by excess bone formation.
items.note: Classic Mendelian phenotype

items.q: In the deep zone of articular cartilage, the collagen fibres are oriented in a:
items.e: The deep (radial) zone has collagen fibres running perpendicular to the surface to resist compressive load.
items.note: Correct, standard anatomical fact.

items.q: Which proteoglycan is most abundant in articular cartilage and is responsible for its compressive stiffness?
items.e: Aggrecan carries the large GAG chains that attract water, giving the cartilage its load‑bearing ability.
items.note: Classic textbook fact.

items.q: Which collagen type is unique to the calcified zone of articular cartilage and is also found in hypertrophic growth plate chondrocytes?
items.e: Type X collagen is expressed in the hypertrophic zone of the growth plate and in calcified cartilage, marking the mineralisation front.
items.note: Consistent with the notes.

items.q: The superficial zone of articular cartilage produces a boundary lubricant that is absent in osteoarthritic cartilage. This protein is:
items.e: Lubricin, secreted by superficial chondrocytes and synoviocytes, reduces friction across the articular surface.
items.note: Standard orthopaedic knowledge.

items.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the water content of articular cartilage?
o: It is highest in the deep zone
It increases with age in all zones
It is highest in the superficial zone
It is uniform across the thickness
items.e: Water content peaks at the surface and drops towards the deep zone; an increase in water content weakens the matrix.
items.note: Definitive, well‑documented.

items.q: During a knee joint load, the fluid phase of cartilage contributes to load‑bearing by:
o: Carrying most of the load initially
Attaching collagen fibres to mineralised tissue
items.e: Biphasic behaviour: fluid pressurisation supports >90 % of the load during the initial phase of loading.
items.note: Accurate biphasic behaviour.

items.q: A 62‑year‑old patient has a femoral shaft fracture fixed with a stainless‑steel intramedullary nail. Three months later the patient presents with a sudden break of the nail under normal walking load. Which factor most likely contributed to this failure?
o: Suboptimal nail–bone contact due to cortical thinning
High fracture shaft bone density leading to fatigue failure below ultimate strength
Excessive external torque applied during a fall
items.e: Intramedullary nails fail predominantly by fatigue when cyclic loads exceed the endurance limit. Cortical thinning reduces stiffness and increases local stress, so sub‑optimal bone‑nail contact is the usual culprit.
items.note: Consistent with fatigue mechanics and noted bone‑implant interaction.

items.q: During a long‑term orthopaedic follow‑up of a patient with a large cortical window created for tumor resection, which defect geometry would be most detrimental to torsional strength?
o: A round hole 8 mm in diameter
A round hole 30 mm in diameter
A longitudinal slot 30 mm long with sharp ends
A thin rim‑seat with a beveled edge
items.e: A longitudinal slot (open‑section defect) removes material from the periosteal surface and drastically reduces torsional resistance—often by >90 %—unlike a round hole.
items.note: Based on documented stress‑riser effects.

items.q: A patient with a femoral neck fracture is being considered for fixation. The surgeon notes that the fracture is located through the cancellous zone adjacent to the bone–cancellous interface. Which statement about the mechanical environment of this fracture is correct?
o: It is exposed to high shear stress due to cancellous bone’s high shear strength
It experiences low torsional stress because cancellous bone is low‑modulus
It is subjected to high compressive stresses because cancellous bone is strongest in compression
It is exposed to high tensile stress due to cortical bone’s superior tension resistance
items.e: Cancellous bone has the lowest modulus and is strongest in compression but weak in tension; therefore a fracture near it will mainly experience high compressive stresses.
items.note: Matches the stress‑pattern table.

items.q: In a prospective cohort study examining the effect of a new physiotherapy protocol on post‑operative shoulder function, which of the following outcomes will give the strongest estimate of the relative risk of improvement?
o: Kaplan‑Meier survival curve for time to return to daily activities
Adjusted odds ratio from logistic regression
Incidence of improvement in the intervention group divided by that in the control group
items.e: The relative risk is obtained by dividing the incidence (probability) of improvement in the intervention group by that in the control group – option C.  An odds ratio (option B) approximates relative risk only when the outcome is rare; a Kaplan‑Meier curve (option A) and risk difference (option D) do not give a relative estimate.
items.note: Correct answer is C; distractors are poorly defined or approximate metrics.

items.q: When designing a pragmatic randomized controlled trial for comparing two total knee arthroplasty implants, which strategy best preserves the external validity of the findings?
o: Using a highly selective inclusion criterion focusing on young, healthy patients
Employing a crossover design so each patient receives both implants
Allowing surgeons to use their preferred surgical technique for each implant
Blinding the surgeons to the implant type
items.e: Pragmatic trials aim to reflect real‑world practice; letting surgeons use the technique they are comfortable with maintains applicability while still randomizing patients to implants.
items.note: Clear single best answer.

items.q: A meta‑analysis of level III studies on ankle fracture fixation reports a pooled odds ratio of 1.8 with a 95 % confidence interval of 0.9 to 3.6. According to GRADE, this evidence should be rated as:
items.e: The wide confidence interval that includes unity indicates imprecision; hence the evidence is downgraded to low.
items.note: GRADE grading matches the notes.

items.q: Which of the following best describes allocation concealment in a randomized controlled trial?
o: Keeping the treatment assignments hidden from outcome assessors
Preventing the enrolling investigator from knowing the next allocation before patient enrolment
Ensuring blinding of the patients to their treatment group
Masking the statistical analysis plan until study completion
items.e: Allocation concealment sequesters the randomisation sequence from the enrolment process to prevent selection bias.
items.note: Correct definition.

items.q: In a case‑control study investigating risk factors for postoperative infections after hip replacement, why is it important to match controls to cases on age?
o: Age is a potential confounder that could distort the association between exposure and outcome
It ensures that the sample size is adequate
It guarantees that exposure distribution is the same in both groups
items.e: Age can influence both the likelihood of receiving a particular intervention and the risk of infection; matching on age controls for this confounder.
items.note: Standard epidemiology principle.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old patient receives a pelvic radiograph. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the tube voltage (kVp) and the patient's dose?
o: Increasing kVp increases the number of photons but reduces the average photon energy
Increasing kVp increases both the number of photons and the average photon energy, raising dose
Changing kVp has no effect on dose, only on image contrast
Increasing kVp decreases both photon number and energy, thereby lowering dose
items.e: Higher kVp produces photons of greater energy, so fewer are absorbed; the tube adjusts mAs to keep image exposure, resulting in a higher dose overall.
items.note: Physics of X‑ray tube.

items.q: During a lumbar spine CT scan, the technician selects a 120 kVp tube voltage. What is the predominant photon interaction in the soft tissues of the lumbar region at this energy?
items.e: At 120 kVp, the photon energy (~60 keV typical for the beam spectrum) is such that Compton scatter dominates in soft tissue.
items.note: Standard CT interaction regime.

items.q: In fluoroscopic arthroscopy of the knee, why is the beam positioned below the table with the image intensifier above the patient?
o: It reduces patient skin dose by lowering entrance dose
It increases scatter back towards the surgeon
It maximises the magnification for the surgeon
It aligns the beam with the patient’s centre of mass
items.e: With the tube beneath the table, the beam enters from below, placing the higher scatter zone (entrance side) away from the surgeon; the intensifier is near the exit side, reducing scatter reaching the surgeon.
items.note: Fluoroscopy geometry.

items.q: A 3‑mm lead apron is advertised. In terms of lead equivalence, this apron attenuates:
items.e: Lead of 3 mm thickness attenuates approximately 95 % of surrounding scatter, making it adequate for routine protection.
items.note: Lead attenuation data.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old man with COPD and a BMI of 41 is scheduled for elective total knee arthroplasty. Which of the following pre‑operative optimisation steps is most strongly associated with a reduced risk of postoperative wound complications?
o: Start prophylactic fluoroquinolone 5 days before surgery
Administer 500 mg oral iron daily for one week
items.e: Pre‑operative glucose control is most strongly linked to wound outcomes; values >200 mg/dL raise infection risk. Smoking cessation improves healing but is less directly tied to glucose‑driven complications.
items.note: All options are plausible but only option C has a clear evidence‑based link to reduced wound complications.

items.q: During a hip fracture fixation under neuraxial anaesthesia, a 70‑year‑old patient is discovered to have severe aortic stenosis. What is the preferred intra‑operative monitoring strategy to minimise hypotensive episodes?
o: Keep arterial line cuff at 200 mmHg
Use Doppler ultrasound for non‑invasive BP only
