Place a central venous line and avoid spinal anaesthesia
Continuous invasive arterial pressure monitoring with a 5 mmHg increment guide
items.e: In aortic stenosis, small BP drops are catastrophic; continuous invasive arterial pressure gives immediate feedback, allowing rapid vasopressor titration.
items.note: Only option D provides the required real‑time monitoring.

items.q: Which of the following statements about vancomycin infusion in orthopaedic patients is correct?
o: It should never be combined with cefazolin for surgical prophylaxis
The infusion can safely be given in 5 min to reduce red‑man syndrome
An infusion time of 1–2 h is recommended to avoid red‑man syndrome
It is nephrotoxic only when used with aminoglycosides
items.e: A slow 1–2 h infusion lowers the risk of red‑man syndrome; rapid infusion precipitates histamine release.
items.note: Option C matches standard guidelines.

items.q: A patient with a known penicillin allergy undergoes an elective arthroplasty. Which of the following is the most appropriate single‑dose prophylactic antibiotic?
items.e: Clindamycin covers most skin flora in penicillin‑allergic patients; cefazolin is contraindicated if immediate hypersensitivity exists.
items.note: Correct answer is unambiguously clindamycin.

items.q: An otherwise healthy 28‑year‑old man lands on his feet from a 3‑metre fall. Radiographs reveal a transcervical femoral neck fracture with a Pauwels III angle. The most appropriate surgical approach is:
o: Closed reduction and three‐cannulated screw fixation via an anterior approach.
Open reduction through a Smith‑Petersen approach and fixation with a dynamic hip screw.
Closed reduction and a cephalomedullary nail with an anti‑rotation screw.
Primary hemiarthroplasty with a short stem.
items.e: Pauwels III fractures are highly vertical; a cephalomedullary nail with an anti‑rotation screw provides fixed‑angle support, converting shear into compression and reducing instability.
items.note: Answer C is the standard treatment for a vertical fracture in a young patient.

items.q: Which of the following is the best predictor of cut‑out when using a dynamic hip screw in an intertrochanteric fracture?
o: Lateral wall thickness greater than 30 mm.
Use of a single lag screw rather than multiple.
items.e: Tip‑apex distance (TAD) >25 mm markedly increases cut‑out risk; keeping it under 25 mm is a key surgical target.
items.note: Standard teaching from Baumgaertner and subsequent studies.

items.q: A 65‑year‑old female with a recent osteoporotic intertrochanteric fracture (AO/OTA 31A2.3) is planned for fixation. What intra‑operative finding would most likely warrant conversion from a dynamic hip screw to a cephalomedullary nail?
o: Intact femoral shaft distal to the lesser trochanter.
Subtrochanteric extension of the fracture line.
Inferior placement of the lag screw in the femoral head.
items.e: Subtrochanteric extension makes a DHS unstable; a cephalomedullary nail provides distal fixation and better control of the proximal fragment.
items.note: Answer C reflects standard practice.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old diabetic patient with a medial tibial plateau fracture (Schatzker IV) shows a popliteal pulse of 60 mmHg and ankle‑brachial index of 0.85. What is the next best step?
o: Proceed to ORIF with lateral approach
Apply a brief spacer and observe
items.e: Popliteal artery injury is a major concern in medial plateau fractures; an arterial study (e.g., duplex) is indicated early.
items.note: Clear vascular indication.

items.q: Which soft‑tissue structure is most commonly injured in a lateral tibial plateau fracture with meniscal incarceration?
items.e: Lateral plateau fractures frequently entrap peripheral lateral meniscus; ACL injuries are also common but not the most typical.
items.note: Distractor MCL less common in lateral fractures.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old woman has a lateral tibial plateau fracture classified as Schatzker IIIb (central depression). What is the preferred fixation method?
o: Internal fixation of the central fragment with a cannulated screw and subchondral bone graft
External fixation through a spanning frame
items.e: Central depressed fractures need subchondral support; a central cannulated screw plus bone graft provides a stable scaffold.
items.note: Single optimal choice.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of an arthrosis‑prone bicondylar tibial plateau fracture (Schatzker V)?
items.e: Open reduction under GA is not a complication; it is the surgical procedure used.
items.note: Clear distinction.

items.q: A patient presents with a distal tibial plafond fracture classified as AO/OTA 43‑C3. What is the first step in the staged management protocol?
o: Proceed to ORIF in a single stage
items.e: For comminuted distal tibial fractures, a spanning external fixator is applied first to restore alignment and allow soft‑tissue healing.
items.note: Standard staged approach.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old patient presents with a Weber B fracture (serrated‑id ankle radiograph shows a fibular fracture at the syndesmotic level). Weight‑bearing mortise film shows a normal medial clear space. The weight‑bearing test is most predictive of
items.e: A normal medial clear space on weight‑bearing radiographs indicates that the syndesmosis is intact, even if the Weber B fracture appears unstable on a non‑weight‑bearing film.
items.note: Consistent with Ottawa rules and Campbell

items.q: During surgical fixation of a perforated lateral ankle screw in a Weber C fracture, the surgeon notices the tibiofibular overlap is ≤1 mm on a mortise view. Which step is most appropriate next?
o: Add a second lag screw through the fibula
Reserve fixation of the lateral malleolus until the syndesmosis is restored
items.e: An overlap ≤1 mm on a mortise view is a reliable sign of syndesmotic injury; urgent syndesmotic fixation is required before finalizing fibular fixation.
items.note: Radiographic criteria verified

items.q: The most common foot position in the Lauge‑Hansen classification of ankle fractures is
items.e: Supination‑external rotation (SER) accounts for roughly 40–75 % of ankle fractures, making supination the most common foot position in this classification.
items.note: Statistical consensus

items.q: A 35‑year‑old swimmer sustains an isolated medial malleolar fracture with a vertical comminution. The best fixation method for this fracture type is
items.e: Vertical (SAD) medial malleolar fractures respond best to an antiglide plate placed on the posterior lateral aspect to provide a stable fixation and allow early motion.
items.note: Biomechanical evidence

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with a displaced 4‑part proximal humeral fracture is best treated with a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty because:
o: It provides predictable function irrespective of tuberosity healing
It prevents avascular necrosis of the humeral head
It is the least expensive option
items.e: In elderly patients the head‑splitting fracture predicts poor tuberosity healing and high AVN risk; RTSA yields consistent function without dependence on tuberosity union.
items.note: All statements align with the notes.

items.q: During ORIF of a 3‑part proximal humerus fracture with a locking plate, the most critical point to avoid varus collapse is:
o: Placing the plate 10 mm above the greater tuberosity
Fixing the lesser tuberosity with a single screw
Ensuring the plate lies above the axillary nerve
items.e: An inferomedial “calcar” screw restores medial support; loss of this support leads to varus collapse and screw cut‑out.
items.note: Matches technical points from the notes.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old footballer sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation with a Hill‑Sachs lesion involving 30% of the posterosuperolateral head. The most appropriate surgical option is:
items.e: In a young athlete, arthroscopic Bankart repair reduces recurrence; a Hill‑Sachs of 30% does not warrant a McLaughlin or arthroplasty.
items.note: Consistent with notes on young athletes and Hill‑Sachs management.

items.q: Which of the following is a key predictor of head ischemia in a proximal humerus fracture according to Hertel?
o: Displacement of >45° of the greater tuberosity
items.e: Hertel’s criteria list a disrupted medial hinge (>2 mm) as a major predictor of avascular necrosis.
items.note: Matches Hertel criteria.

items.q: A 16‑year‑old footballer presents with a painful, swollen left elbow after a fall onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show an intra‑articular fracture involving the entire radial head and a small fragment of the capitellum. Which surgical option is most appropriate?
o: Open reduction and internal fixation of the radial head with headless screws only
Radial head replacement arthroplasty with a metal monopolar stem
Excision of the radial head followed by reconstruction of the interosseous membrane
Closed reduction and immobilisation for 6 weeks
items.e: The fracture is a Mason type III (comminuted whole head). Mason III fractures requiring ORIF with more than three fragments are best treated by radial head arthroplasty to avoid poor fixation and instability.
items.note: Straightforward, single‑best answer supported by reference.

items.q: Which radiographic sign is pathognomonic for a Mason II radial head fracture with a mechanical block in a stable elbow?
o: Double‑arc sign on the lateral view
Posterior fat‑pad sign on the lateral view
Absent capitellum on the AP view
Lateral subluxation of the radial head on the AP view
items.e: The double‑arc sign on the lateral radiograph indicates a displaced single fragment of the radial head (Mason II) causing a mechanical block to motion.
items.note: Single radiographic marker; distractors describe other classic signs.

items.q: An elderly patient with a displaced, non‑comminuted transverse olecranon fracture is brought to the OR. What is the most appropriate fixation technique?
o: Tension‑band wiring with two parallel K‑wires and figure‑of‑eight wire
Dorsal pre‑contoured plate with locking screws
Conservative splinting with protected early motion
items.e: A transverse, non‑comminuted olecranon fracture is ideally fixed with tension‑band wiring, which converts triceps tension into compression across the articular surface.
items.note: Standard treatment; distractors are clearly inferior.

items.q: Which of the following is a recognised predictor of loss of reduction in a cast for distal radius fractures in adults?
items.e: Lafontaine’s criteria list dorsal angulation >20° as one of the red flags for cast failure.
items.note: Dorsal angulation >20° on the lateral view is one of Lafontaine’s predictors of cast failure; the other options are not classified as such.

items.q: In a Baxter’s (Barton's) fracture, the ‘critical corner’ fragment is:
o: A dorsal rim of the lunate facet that is small and distal
The volar rim of the scaphoid
items.e: The volar lunate facet fragment, if missed, leads to volar carpal subluxation and requires fixation distal to the watershed line.
items.note: The ‘critical corner’ fragment in a Barton's fracture is the small distal volar lunate‑facet fragment; missing it leads to volar carpal subluxation.

items.q: Which fracture pattern of the scaphoid is associated with the highest risk of avascular necrosis?
items.e: The proximal pole receives most of its blood supply retrogradely from the dorsal branch; fractures here carry the highest AVN risk.
items.note: The proximal pole receives the majority of its retrograde blood supply and has the highest AVN risk.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old male sustains a displaced distal radius fracture with 2 mm articular step‑off. According to current consensus, the optimal fixation method is:
items.e: Articular step‑off >2 mm warrants operative fixation; a volar locking plate provides stable purchase and restores the articular surface.
items.note: Articular step‑off >2 mm is an operative indication; volar locking plate provides stable restoration.

items.q: Which complication is most likely after a volar plating of a distal radius fracture when the plate is placed too distal to the watershed line?
items.e: A volar plate distal to the watershed line can irritate the flexor pollicis longus, leading to tendon rupture.
items.note: A volar plate placed too distal to the watershed line irritates the FPL tendon, the most common tendon rupture complication.

items.q:
A 65‑year‑old man with a Gustilo‑Anderson type IIIB open tibial fracture has been stabilised with external fixation. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate according to current BOAST/BAPRAS‑BOA standards?
A) Cefazolin 1 g IV every 12 h for 24 h total
B) Cefazolin 1 g IV every 8 h plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV in the first 12 h, followed by cefazolin for 24 h
C) Ceftriaxone 2 g IV once plus clindamycin 600 mg IV every 8 h for 5 days
D) Ampicillin‑sulbactam 2.5 g IV every 6 h for 72 h
items.e: Type IIIB wounds need gram‑negative coverage; the evidence‑based regimen is cefazolin with gentamicin for the first 12 h, then cefazolin alone for up to 24 h. The duration must not exceed 72 h, and the total antibiotic course should stop once the wound is definitively covered.
items.note: "B" is the only option that follows BOAST/BAPRAS‑BOA guidance.

items.q: During the management of an acetabular fracture, a surgeon chooses a sliding compression plate to obtain relative stability. Which of the following best explains why this hardware will encourage callus formation?
o: It generates absolute stability by allowing interfragmentary compression
It permits controlled load sharing and micromotion within the 2–10 % strain window
It completely eliminates motion, preventing strain‑induced osteogenesis
It recruits osteogenic growth factors directly to the fracture site
items.e: A sliding compression plate does not provide absolute compression; instead, it allows a small amount of micromotion (2–10 %) that lies within the strain range for secondary healing, thereby stimulating callus formation.
items.note: Question and answer are factually correct

items.q: A 55‑year‑old smoker presents with a 3‑cm diaphyseal gap non‑union of the humerus after a failed plating. Which treatment strategy is most consistent with the diamond concept for achieving union?
o: Re‑serve the existing plate and wash the site with saline
Replace the plate with a larger, more rigid construct and add a vascularized fibular graft
Perform a double‑tubular external fixator with >1 mm distraction per day
Apply a simple casting immobilization without bone graft
items.e: The diamond concept integrates mechanical stability, biologic augmentation, and a vascularized graft. A larger rigid plate provides stability, while a vascularized fibula supplies osteogenic cells and blood flow, fitting the four pillars of the concept.
items.note: Correct application of the diamond concept

items.q: In the context of Perren’s strain theory, which of the following statements is **FALSE** regarding fracture healing?
o: Strain <2 % generally leads to primary bone healing without a callus
Strain between 2–10 % promotes secondary healing with callus formation
Strain >10 % but <100 % favors fibrous tissue formation
Strain >100 % is required for successful endochondral ossification
items.e: Endochondral ossification occurs within the 2–10 % strain window of secondary healing, not at strains >100 %. High strain (>100 %) usually produces granulation tissue and risk of non‑union.
items.note: Standard Perren strain thresholds

items.q: A 30‑year‑old woman has a displaced intra‑articular calcaneal fracture. Which fixation principle is most critical to avoid post‑traumatic arthritis?
o: Absolute stability with an articular fragment lag screw
Relative stability using a bridging plate
Maximum lengthening of the foot to relieve pressure
items.e: In intra‑articular fractures, absolute stability with a lag screw preserves the joint surface and prevents cartilage damage, whereas relative stability or bridging approaches would allow motion at the articular surface.
items.note: Intra‑articular fracture demands absolute stability

items.q: A 45‑year‑old diabetic patient presents with a comminuted femoral shaft fracture. The surgeon chooses intramedullary nailing. What perioperative factor is most likely to impede the biological aspect of the diamond concept in this patient?
o: Use of a titanium nail instead of stainless steel
Placement of a single lag screw in the distal fragment
items.e: Hyperglycaemia in diabetes reduces osteoblast activity and vascularity, compromising the biological arm of the diamond concept. Material choice and fixation technique are less directly related to biological impairment.
items.note: Diabetes is a known biological modifier

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised risk factor for atypical femoral fracture in bisphosphonate users?
o: Long duration of bisphosphonate therapy (>5 years)
Use of high‑dose IV zoledronate for oncology
items.e: Atypical femoral fractures develop after prolonged bisphosphonate exposure, not after recent initiation. High‑dose oncology regimens and long‑term use are risk factors.
items.note: Stem and options correctly reflect guideline‑based risk factors.

items.q: Which supplement is required before initiating IV zoledronate therapy?
items.e: Vitamin D deficiency predisposes to hypocalcaemia after zoledronate; patients should be vitamin D replete (2000 IU daily) before the infusion.
items.note: Stem reflects usual pre‑infusion requirement.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old man presents with painless, progressive enlargement of his frontal skull. Plain radiographs show a mix of lytic and sclerotic zones with diploic widening. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised while calcium and phosphate are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: The classic combination of raised ALP with normal calcium, skull enlargement and mixed lytic‑sclerotic changes is diagnostic of Paget disease.
items.note: Standard radiographic and biochemical features match Paget.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman has knee pain and antero‑medial bowing of the femur. Plain film shows a thick, enlarged femur with a “candle flame” lytic front. Blood work reveals normal calcium, phosphate and a total ALP of 180 U/L (normal 40‑120). What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
o: Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV single dose
items.e: In active Paget disease, a single IV dose of zoledronic acid is the most effective initial treatment, abolishing pain and lowering ALP.
items.note: IV bisphosphonate is the guideline‑recommended initial therapy.

items.q: Which complication is *least* likely in a patient with extensive polyostotic Paget disease?
o: Sudden onset neuropathic pain at a remote site
items.e: While cardiac failure, deafness and basilar invagination are recognized sequelae, neuropathic pain at a remote site is not a typical complication of Paget disease.
items.note: Other options are classic complications.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old man with known Paget disease of the pelvis develops a sudden, excruciating hip pain. X‐ray shows a transverse, subtrochanteric fracture that failed to heal after 6 months. What is the most likely reason for the delayed union?
o: Excessive blood flow causing a steal phenomenon
Intrinsic mechanical weakness of pagetic bone
items.e: Pagetic bone is enlarged but mechanically weak; this makes transverse fractures, especially subtrochanteric, prone to non‑union regardless of remodeling activity.
items.note: Biomechanical weakness of pagetic bone is the established cause.

items.q: During investigation of a suspected paget’s sarcoma, which MRI finding would most strongly argue against a malignant change?
o: Preservation of marrow fat and absence of a mass
items.e: In uncomplicated Paget disease, marrow fat remains on MRI. Loss of fat signal and a soft‑tissue mass would raise suspicion for sarcoma.
items.note: Marrow fat preservation is a key benign feature.

items.q: A patient with monostotic Paget disease of the femur has an ALP of 110 U/L but a normal liver function panel. Which additional test should be ordered to confirm that the elevated ALP is from bone?
items.e: Bone‑specific ALP distinguishes bone from liver origins when total ALP is only mildly raised.
items.note: Specific isoform assay is the standard confirmatory test.
